We discuss what teams get wrong when adopting microservices, why independent deployment matters, and how microservices can help teams work more autonomously.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>We also peek into his new book, ‘</span><strong><a underline;">Building Resilient Distributed Systems</a></strong><span>’, and Sam explains his three rules for distributed systems, why observability is essential, and also why it’s vital to take business context into account when deciding whether to fail open or fail closed on errors.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px plaintext;">We also explore how AI is changing software development, from specs versus code as a source of truth to cognitive debt and cognitive surrender. Sam shares how modular architecture can help teams experiment with AI while maintaining understanding of the systems being built.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Takeaways from the conversation with Sam</strong></h3><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/a93ad983-dfa5-4c09-a380-054a16bc3d68?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/a0sZV0qIbI0" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>1. In the room when “microservices” was coined. </strong><span>In the early years of the 2010s, James Lewis – Sam’s colleague at Thoughtworks – kept running into companies building service-oriented architectures where each service could be replaced quickly. At an architecture symposium in the Lake District, England, James pitched a name for this trend: “micro apps,” and in a room of about 10 people (including Sam), someone else suggested “microservices.” Lewis and Martin Fowler then wrote the first article on the topic in March 2014, ‘</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0b82fd3c-2f03-4e05-b637-66ca22b7ac03?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Microservices: a definition of this new architectural term</a><span>’, and Sam published the book </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/227fe736-f9a7-4cd8-b7a5-ae0a8b2e0ccc?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Building Microservices</a><span> the following year.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>2. Sam spent 18 months teaching Googlers how to write good automated tests. </strong><span>In 2007, Sam was embedded at Yahoo and Google as a ThoughtWorks consultant, alongside people from Pivotal Labs. Their job was to teach engineers how to write automated tests, and code that’s testable. He recalls that some Google devs did not believe it was possible to write automated functional tests for websites, until Sam and his colleagues showed them how Selenium works!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>3. Sam spent 10+ years at a large company, three years at startups, and has been independent for more than a decade.</strong><span> After 13 years at Thoughtworks, he quit to avoid becoming “institutionalized.” He recalls thinking he could hang around at Thoughtworks and grow bitter. “So I’ll just go now.” He then worked at three different startups before going independent, which he’s now done for 15 years. The biggest challenge of being your own boss? He says: “The problem of working for yourself is that the boss is frequently an a*****e. So, current Sam frequently is cursing past Sam for the commitments he made!”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>4. So, what’s a “microservice?” </strong><span>Sam gives two definitions: a clear one, and a softer one:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Independently deployable service. </strong><span>The “clear” definition: as long as, upon a change to a system, it can be independently deployed – without any other services needing to be deployed –, you can call it a microservice.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Clear boundaries around the business domain.</strong><span> The “softer” definition: services split by business function (not by technical layer) can also be called microservices.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>5. Three rules of distributed systems: </strong><span>Sam sometimes struggled to recall the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ec10fcf8-bca0-40fa-aedf-8acf63565a99?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">eight fallacies of distributed computing</a><span>, and so he boiled them down to the three that cause the most problems:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">1. Information takes time to travel. You cannot send information instantaneously from point A to point B. This is basically the “speed of light” constraint.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">2. Sometimes, the thing you want to talk to isn’t there. That is, resources can and do go offline.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">3. Resources are not infinite; you will eventually run out of things like CPU, memory, storage, and networking bandwidth.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In Sam’s experience, most distributed systems outages are caused by #3; resource pools running out.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>6. Dealing with idempotency: keys or fingerprints? </strong><span>Idempotency is performing the same operation multiple times and it having the same effect as if done once only. For example, if you repeatedly hit the “down” button for an elevator, nothing more happens than what happened upon that first press: multiple button smashes don’t bring more elevators your way. Payments are a classic example where idempotency is needed: when you retry or refresh a payments page, you should not be charged twice.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">There are two common ways to deal with idempotency:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Idempotency keys</strong><span>: a client sends a unique identifier (usually a UUID) that is the idempotency key. The server makes sure operations with the same idempotency key are executed only once. It’s clean to build but hard to retrofit, which involves changing both the client and server.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Fingerprints:</strong><span> the client sends nothing, but the server creates a “fingerprint” of the request by hashing relevant fields. It’s easy to retrofit later (only need to change the server), however, legitimate requests can be rejected as duplicates, and duplicate requests could still happen. Sam  describes a Danish payment system he worked on that rejected purchases of the same value within a 5-minute period while it did the fingerprinting.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>7. Four concepts of resiliency:</strong><span> Sam frequently references the four outcomes for military systems, explained </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/708e12d8-3548-4db7-9570-1f3adc7bf209?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">by David Woods</a><span>:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Robustness</strong><span>: systems continue to function as intended, for example, when Kubernetes replaces a failing pod. A downside of robustness is that it can add complexity, and more complex systems have more ways to fail.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Rebound</strong><span>: how quickly the system recovers when something goes wrong.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Extensibility</strong><span>: dealing with surprises and being able to stretch the system’s support to deal with new needs</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Adaptability</strong><span>: the system changing to support new functions. Resilient systems are adapted, even between incidents.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>8. What if code is a side effect of collaboration? </strong><span>When Sam was at Thoughtworks, some clients refused to do pair programming as a practice because they could only see one developer typing and the other doing nothing, which is a waste. Martin Fowler’s dictum that “programming is not typing” helped Sam to explain to clients that typing out code is an output, but not an outcome.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Sam conceives programming as building a system collectively, and code is one of the mechanisms delivering the system. Now that with LLMs we no longer spend most time typing out code, we’ll discover the next bottleneck in creating good software. Could it be delayed feedback cycles?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>9. Hedging the vendor options is sensible when integrating AI into systems. </strong><span>It’s hard to tell which AI companies have long-term, sustainable business models and which don’t, so it’s the responsible thing when designing systems to hedge the providers. Aim to be multi-vendor, multi-model in your choices, so you can easily change the vendor or model layer. Also, consider if you can swap out LLM-powered functionality for deterministic code that runs faster and cheaper.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>10. We must resist “cognitive surrender” to AI. </strong><span>Sam believes that more AI usage is leading to less critical thinking – or could we be using it wrong? He says: “The original pitch of AI was it was going to free us from drudgery. We’d have less toil, and we can focus more on critical thinking and smarts. However, much of our current use of AI is not freeing us up from critical thinking! It’s causing </span><em>more</em><span> context switching and leaving less time for thinking. People are working longer hours; we’ve got studies that show this.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">But [longer hours and more context switching] is not necessarily AI’s fault. It’s just how we’re using it.”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Putting in the effort often leads to better results. For example, when writing Building Resilient Distributed Systems, Sam used NotebookLM for research, but he manually clicked through each link it surfaced, and checked whether it was information he wanted to reference.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>11. Starting with modules encourages better software architecture. Also: production is truth. </strong><span>I asked Sam for advice on what to do to get better at designing systems:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Start by thinking carefully about module boundaries and the connections between them</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><span>When you use AI, allow it to roam freely, but only </span><em>inside</em><span> the module structure that you have designed!</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>12. Much of the tech world might still be naive about what an LLM is. </strong><span>As Sam said:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“I think the tech world in general is quite naive about AI and fundamentally misunderstands what an LLM is. For example: why did the LLM delete my database? Well, because it has no concept of causality. They have no concept that if I do A, B happens.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">LLMs are not world models. World models have been around for a long time. They predate LLMs. So if you had the appropriate model and the appropriate inputs, world models could at least get to the point of ‘if I do X, then Y happens and I’ve been told not to do Y.’ </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>I think we expect LLMs to do more than they actually can do, because they seem so smart.</strong><span> This leads us to overestimate their capabilities a bit too much. But the nature of LLMs is why all the guardrails around LLMs are really not going to be the right long-term solution.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Sam’s comments feel very timely, given Opus 5.5 </span><a none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Recommendations are one of the most important pieces of the Netflix experience. If you’ve watched Netflix, you would have noticed the Netflix homepage recommending a bunch of movies and TV shows. More often than not, they happen to be stuff that might be of interest to you. They also keep changing with time based on what you’ve watched.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The original Netflix recommendations engine was built on top of 1000s of hand‑crafted features across users, items, and interactions. It also used special architecture for various functions that contributed to the task of making recommendations.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Though a lot of changes have happened to this stack over the years, it’s still pretty complex. It’s costly to onboard new use cases. At the same time, large language models (LLMs) have made great strides. They have progressed a lot in their ability to recommend things to a user. Due to their broader world knowledge and understanding of language, LLMs do a good job of figuring out relationships between different things. They can also make recommendations using natural language, which is a plus point. However, you cannot just pick an LLM off-the-shelf to generate recommendations for a company like Netflix.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This is why the Netflix engineering team built GenRec.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The basic idea behind GenRec is to use an LLM to make better sense of a user’s viewing history to assign scores to the various movies and TV shows streaming on Netflix. However, you can’t just give a general-purpose LLM a list of movies or shows that a user has watched and expect it to come up with interesting recommendations. Netflix has to make a bunch of adjustments to the base model to make it work with their content and member behavior.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In this article, we will look at how GenRec was built. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Basic Question with Recommendations</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A recommendation system has to answer a basic question: What should appear first in the list of recommendations?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The answer to this question is the key to deciding which items to show a particular person and in what order. On Netflix, those items can include movies, series, games, and other content types.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The order of the recommendations is super important. A user’s attention span is limited. A viewer might check only a few titles before making a choice. If they don’t find something interesting in that time, they might even leave the platform to check elsewhere. It doesn’t matter if something that the user might like is present in the catalog. You can say that the recommendation system has failed to do its job.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The ordering of the recommendations is handled by a component known as the ranker. It assigns scores to various items based on how suitable they appear for a particular user in a particular situation. The better an item’s score, the higher it appears on the recommendation list. To decide this score, a ranker needs a lot of information. Here are some examples:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">The member’s interaction history to understand what they like or dislike.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Item metadata to make sense of what a piece of content is about.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Details about the device the viewer is using. Time of day. Language or region.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix’s GenRec is capable of ranking the full content catalog. It can also work with a smaller set of content choices that are provided to it. You can use the top-K ranking, which means the highest-ranked K items. Here, K is the number of items you need.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The goal goes beyond predicting what the user will click or play next. Netflix wants to recommend content that can satisfy a user so that they keep coming back for more. This means that a user playing a movie is a great indicator that the user was interested in that recommendation. But it doesn’t guarantee that the recommendation was valuable.</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7c061ce8-d799-46d6-b1f8-a79eb7c59fb0?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">AI’s Next Bottleneck Is Deployment. relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why Netflix Wanted a New Approach</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix already has some very sophisticated recommendation models. Its production systems use thousands of features, representations, and specialized model components. You can think of a feature as an input signal that helps a model make some prediction. For example, we can tell a recommendation model how many comedy movies or shows a user has watched recently. Similarly, we can tell the model how long ago a user has seen a particular piece of content. Or how frequently the user finishes a series. All these features can help the model predict what the user might want to see.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">To create a new feature, you need to decide which observations are important and how to calculate their value. Also, how to make them available for training and prediction. This is known as feature engineering. A mature system also needs a way to make sense of a sequence of actions that a user might perform. For example, if a user has watched several episodes of a series in order, it tells something different from a user starting several unrelated shows, but not watching them after some time.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Over time, these systems keep getting more complex. If you want to support a new content type or a new product surface, you need to add more features. You also need to change the model architecture and perform infrastructure work. Also, you need to run multiple experiments to make sure everything runs fine.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Netflix engineering team wanted to see whether a broadly capable LLM can take on more of this interpretation work. Instead of engineering so many separate signals, the system can describe relevant behavior and content in plain text. The model can be trained to interpret it.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why a Language Model Can Help</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">An LLM has learned a lot of relationships between words, concepts, and descriptions during its training.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This means that the LLM has a much better starting point to make sense of movies and shows and how people interact with them. For example, you can have two movies that belong to different categories but they share themes. An LLM can understand this connection based on their descriptions. It can also make sense of the history of actions that a user has done for movie.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix calls this process of expressing the information in text as verbalization.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">However, a general-purpose LLM is not a good recommender. There are several problems. It may favor globally popular titles. It might suggest items that are not part of the catalog. Also, it doesn’t support personalization. This is why Netflix didn’t go for any off-the-shelf LLM. Instead, the engineering team built GenRec.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">GenRec mixes the language understanding of an LLM with special training that helps it work with the Netflix catalog. The LLM provides a foundation for interpreting the data. But Netflix still has to teach it what a good recommendation looks like and control which items it can recommend.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Two Training Phases of GenRec</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix trained GenRec in two phases with different purposes. Let’s look at both phases in detail.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Phase 1: Develop a Netflix-aware foundation</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This phase is to make GenRec familiar with the domain. The team makes the model learn and interpret Netflix-related information. Only then is it trained for the specific task of ranking recommendations.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Netflix engineering team starts with an open-source foundation LLM and adapts it using proprietary Netflix data. You can think of a foundation model as a broadly useful model that can support multiple applications. After this step, the model gains knowledge of Netflix content and user behavior.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This newly trained model becomes a starting point for multiple lines of work. This model is quite stable. Netflix updates it only after some time period. Not frequently.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Phase 2: Train the Model to Rank</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The second phase turns the foundational LLM into GenRec.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In this phase, the team trains the model on specific examples and objectives. The aim is to rank things properly based on reward signals. Also, while meeting the cost targets.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">We can call this phase post-training, meaning additional training that makes an existing model better for a specific job. Netflix runs this phase more frequently because you need to keep evolving things as new movies and shows are released. Also, viewer choices change. Even a model with strong general knowledge has to keep itself updated based on the latest trends.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How User Behaviour Helps Create Training Examples</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix records many kinds of user interactions. For example, click pays, viewing time, thumbs-up or thumbs-down feedback, adding to watchlist, and abandoned viewing sessions. These records are rich material for creating training examples.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The team turns these examples into conversations. The “user message” contains the member’s history, context, metadata, and the recommendation task. The “assistant message” describes what action the user performed. For example, you can have the input talk about a user who recently completed several mystery episodes, gave positive feedback, and is now watching TV in the evening. The output could talk about the next show this user watched, how long they watched, and whether they gave any feedback.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">As you can see, the output tells what happened next in a particular situation. This helps the model relate what happened before with what happened next. The conversations are just a format to make training easy. It’s not like the users must also chat with Netflix to get recommendations.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">There is a big difference between training and actual use. While training, the conversation format makes it easy to achieve language objectives. While actual use, GenRec receives the context to score movies and TV shows based on the ranking component.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Context Engineering: Choosing What the Model Gets to Read</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">LLMs process text in the form of tokens. They are pieces of text such as words or parts of words.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The amount of tokens we send to the model have an impact on the cost. It also consumes the context budget. This means that describing a user’s entire activity history would be expensive. This leads to a new engineering problem. We need to decide what information to include in the prompt.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/11ced60a-4c28-4924-b508-e30b6b6c71d6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;text-decoration: underline;display: block;"><img class="wide-image" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix calls this context engineering. While building the context, they take into account how useful a particular event is and how much text might be required to put it into words. Some key factors are taken into account:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Strong evidence:</strong><span> Some actions provide strong evidence about a user’s preferences. A long viewing session or explicit positive feedback may deserve a detailed description. Other actions may be less informative. Let’s say a very short viewing or quick hover might reflect accidental or casual exploration. The team omits such events to avoid spending tokens on analyzing weak evidence.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Repetitive behavior: </strong><span>You can represent repeated actions in a more compact manner. For example, if the user has gone through many similar episodes, you can summarize this as a long viewing session of a specific series.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Selective details: </strong><span>Some items need more explanation than others. For example, let’s say we have a new movie with very little interaction history. This is like a cold start. In this case, we need to provide richer metadata.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Context length: </strong><span>The team tests how ranking quality is modified as more historical events are included. Initially, additional history helps a lot. But over time, the improvements become smaller.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix adjusts how many words should be used to describe an event. Using techniques such as cleaning, compression, and word changes, they report that tokens have been reduced to roughly 1/3rd of the original amount.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">What GenRec Learns During Training</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">GenRec brings together multiple training objectives. Each objective addresses a different requirement.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">You can think of a training objective as a way to describe what the model should improve. Improvement is guide through a numerical loss value. Training adjusts the model’s parameters to reduce the loss value.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Let’s look at the key training objectives in detail.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Learning Which Items Should Rank Highly</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This is the primary objective. It teaches GenRec to assign higher scores to each movie or show in the catalog.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix identifies positive examples using engagements such as long playtime or strong feedback. They also apply thresholds and filtering to reduce noise in those labels. It’s important to do so because an action is not always a reliable sign of user preference. You cannot treat every brief play of a movie or show as equally important. They also penalize the model when it assigns too little probability to a relevant catalog item among the available alternatives.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Preserving Language Understanding</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix also keeps a language-modeling objective over the text used in training.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This helps the model make sense of user history, understand more about movies and shows, and act on instructions expressed in natural language. In other words, recommendation training should preserve the language capabilities that make a foundation model useful.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The team has also kept open the possibility of future text applications. For example, explaining recommendations.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Giving More Influence to Important Outcomes</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">You also need the model to not give excessive influence to some specific events. For example, repeated binge-watching can produce multiple events. But this doesn’t mean that you give it excessive weight. Otherwise, the system could become too focused on one type of content.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix addresses this using reward-weighted training.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">They have separate reward models that provide signals about the value of certain engagements. There are signals that contribute to longer-term outcomes. For example, return behavior, exploration, continuous engagement, etc. Other signals help balance out behavior across different types of content, new movie releases, and other trending titles.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How the Model Produces a Ranked List</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Once trained, GenRec can transform a text description into scores for movies and TV shows in the Netflix catalog.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">First, a component known as the verbalizer brings together the user’s watch history, current context, and relevant metadata into a bunch of text. The LLM processes this text sequence and produces internal numerical representations.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix also extracts a pooled hidden state. This is a compact numerical representation of the information that makes sense for a recommendation request. “Pooled” means that information from the model’s processing is collected in a way that another component can use. Don’t think of it as a written summary.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Each catalog item has a learned representation. It also has a learned embedding. You can think of an embedding as a list of numbers a machine-learning model can work with.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Therefore, the model has a clear idea of the user’s current situation and a representation of each item it needs to consider. A scoring head connects the two. You can think of the head as an output component attached to the main model. GenRec’s ranking head combines the user’s context representation with a movie or show’s embedding to generate a score.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Some scoring functions include a dot product or a small neural network. The key idea is that the scoring function learns how the two representations are related. GenRec converts the various scores into a distribution using softmax and uses them to order the recommendation items. Softmax also changes scores into nonnegative values. All of them have a sum of one across the scored set.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Netflix engineering team trains the main LLM, ranking head, and catalog item embeddings together so that they learn to support the same task. Since the head scores only the Netflix catalog items, it cannot recommend something that is not available in the catalog.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How GenRec Makes Recommendations</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">GenRec doesn’t generate recommendations word by word. To understand how it works, you need to understand how a typical text-generating LLM works. It has two stages:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">First, it processes the input prompt. This stage is commonly called prefill.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Next, it generates output tokens one after another. Each new token depends on the earlier context. This stage is called autoregressive decoding.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">GenRec uses the first stage to understand the recommendation context. It then gets the scores from the ranking head.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 href="https://substack.com/redirect/b42c8c3e-f43d-46dd-be8f-b48b60ba9080?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;">Netflix Tech Blog</a></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix describes this as prefill-only inference. In this approach, we process the prompt just once. The model scores the catalog or candidate set in a single forward pass without generating an answer token by token. There is no cost of making the LLM write out a recommendation list.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The engineering team at Netflix serves GenRec using vLLM. It’s software for running LLM workloads. It also keeps the costs in control through smaller or distilled models. You can think of a distilled model as a smaller model trained to learn the behavior of a larger model. The idea is to get high-quality results with lower computational costs.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Netflix also structures prompts to maximize shared prefixes so that prefix caching becomes easy. When requests start with identical text, work done for that shared beginning can be reused. In Netflix’s experiments, when context length was roughly reduced to 1/3rd, it also produced a similar reduction in serving cost.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How Netflix Evaluates GenRec</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Netflix engineering team evaluates GenRec both offline and through a live A/B test. Both methods are for covering different angles.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Offline evaluation is to check whether GenRec ranks known relevant items well. To handle this, the team uses recorded data to measure ranking quality before running a live experiment. One metric that is used is the Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR). It rewards the model when it puts the first relevant item at the top of a ranked list.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/e8f0c63a-ade7-47bc-a4f1-64d10c620b02?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;text-decoration: underline;display: block;"><img class="wide-image" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table><figcaption class="image-caption" style="box-sizing: content-box;color: rgb(119,119,119);font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><span>Source:</span><strong> </strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b42c8c3e-f43d-46dd-be8f-b48b60ba9080?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;">Netflix Tech Blog</a></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Online evaluation checks if making a change has a positive impact on the usage.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In an A/B test, different groups gets different versions of a system so that we can compare the results. Netflix ran a test that covered approx 10% of traffic over 4 weeks. There was an improvement of 0.115% in a short-term homepage engagement metric and 0.006% in a long-term core metric. Netflix labels both results as statistically significant.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Conclusion</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The best takeaway you can have from this case study on GenRec is a shift in how modern recommendation systems are being built.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">If you look at Netflix, it’s clear that most of the input design work involves context engineering. Developers have to decide which user interactions are important. Also, how far back they should look for data. The metadata that should be used. And how to represent everything efficiently.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">We can also have more applications that share a foundation model. Things that can vary are data, the objectives during post-training, reward signals, and the way they provide outputs. The infrastructure also changes with the model. Concerns like GPU serving, batching, caching, etc, are more important.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">GenRec shows how all of these ideas can fit together in an enterprise working at scale:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">The foundation model comes with language and domain understanding</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Context engineering helps give the relevant data to the model.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Specialized training teaches recommendation quality.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Prefill-only serving keeps a check on a major source of inference cost.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>References:</strong></p><ul style="margin-top: Speed of change</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">People in tech are more than used to change; seeing the internet go from zero to everywhere, the arrival of mobile communications and smartphones exploding in popularity, cloud computing rising from a niche concern, and the development of programming languages like Go and Rust, and frameworks like React (web) and Jetpack Compose (Android).</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Despite this, the scale and pace of the impact AI is having at present is still without precedent. That’s how industry veteran Martin Fowler described it </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0120cce5-dfe4-47e2-87cb-a6019d631b8e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">at The Pragmatic Summit</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>“</span><strong>Nothing has hit with the magnitude of AI.</strong><span> This is a whole size difference from anything that we’ve faced before.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">On a smaller scale, we were very much involved in the growth of object-oriented languages. [object-oriented languages] scared a lot of people, but it didn’t scare us so much because we were part of it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The internet had a huge impact upon us all. And, of course, we were spreading the challenge of agile software development. [Agile] had a very big impact on a lot of organizations because you could tell by how hard they resisted it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">But [for all those other changes] we kept talking about how important they were and how valuable they were and trying to persuade people of the importance of them. It may sound surprising, but even for the internet, there were people who wouldn’t think that was important!</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>For AI there’s no argument about how important it is. </strong><span>You cannot put blinkers on to deny the importance of this thing.”</span></p></blockquote><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table Personally, I’m excited by the new opportunity that AI creates, and it’s exciting to experience this revolution firsthand. As mentioned in that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/56a1db33-daa2-47a6-b47a-248df57149aa?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">deepdive</a><span>, I’m certain that my way of coding will change drastically in 2026, and there’ll be plenty of knock-on effects.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>For more on this topic, check out this recent edition of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6bc43bba-a968-46ea-9caf-f715d26a7dfc?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pulse</a><span>.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">#2 Working with several parallel agents is increasingly common</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>I like talking to engineers at AI labs because their working practices are often a few months ahead of the rest of the industry. Claude Code creator, Boris Cherny, revealed the new way he gets things done </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cebcf169-c62d-4c3b-a8a4-85b186f81fbd?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">on the podcast:</a></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>“</span><strong>I have 5 terminal tabs.</strong><span> Each one of them has a checkout of their repository. I’ll round robin and start Claude Code in each one. I also run 5-10 Claudes on Claude Web, in parallel with my local Claudes.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>A few months after these comments, on </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e6010c5c-8118-44cb-959a-9282f5f80b3b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">last week’s pod</a><span> with Cockroach Labs cofounder, Peter Mattis, – who’s an extremely productive developer who wrote circa 100K lines of code/year, pre-AI – said he’s doing something similar:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>“Oftentimes, I’m doing things in parallel. </span><strong>I find my cognitive overhead is about 5-10 agent sessions concurrently.</strong><span> But sometimes those sessions will have many subagents doing things.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">I also asked a former coworker at Uber, who’s also an extremely productive software engineer, how he works these days. Dima Zaytsev (now a software engineer at Linear), told me:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“⁠It used to be a simple world: one mouse, one keyboard, one screen. You physically can’t work on more than one thing at once. Now, you no longer have that limitation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>I end up having 5-10 (literally) worktrees locally that I rotate between.</strong><span> Prompt one agent, and while it is working, move on to another to test output or review code.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Nearly all of the most productive software engineers I’ve met – who were hand-writing code a year ago – no longer write the code by hand and also run several parallel agents. What a change!</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A software engineer at a mid-sized startup told me something that’s pretty much an open secret across the industry, including at places with code reviews in place.</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>“</span><strong>Everyone is playing the theater of doing reviews</strong><span>, but with the volume of changes that get thrown your way, I observed that people just find a path of least resistance: give up on reviews and just stamp everything with LGTM.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">We are gradually phasing out this process ourselves with some shortcuts that you are allowed to take, and that has been a major productivity boost.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">At the LDX3 conference, there was a strong reaction among the audience when they heard the bolded sentence out above. Today at most companies, there is indeed a “theater of code reviews”. The fact is that no engineer can keep up with 5-10 times more code to review, so most don’t thoroughly review the code.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight:
