As Mario Zechner, the creator of Pi, said </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7b211f84-df4d-4c2e-a1a0-f16e61154c12?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">on the podcast</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“Everything is broken. It sure feels like software has become a brittle mess, with 98% uptime becoming the norm instead of the exception, including for big services. And user interfaces have the weirdest bugs that you’d think a QA team would catch. I give you that that’s been the case for longer than agents exist. But we seem to be accelerating.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>We covered the phenomenon of quality being worse with more AI usage in March, in ‘</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ffb653c9-53b8-4730-b25a-378be64fa7b5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Are AI agents actually slowing us down?</a><span>’</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Infra capacity shortage</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>It’s common knowledge that there’s a GPU shortage and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5820f5da-aad9-4f44-8a8e-fd6727c24667?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">memory shortage</a><span> in the market. In addition, there’s also the growing trend of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/93bfb5ba-bfb1-4d4b-81c0-6d3d98b7727b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">CPU shortages</a><span>. As I covered last month:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“Apparently, it’s now nearly impossible to get CPUs on spot instances without long-running connections with cloud providers. Also, reserving specific CPUs now needs to be done months in advance, and cloud providers will even turn down certain reservations because they don’t have enough CPUs or the right type of CPUs.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>If you’re at a company with a non-trivial amount of CPU usage, securing capacity is something worth doing now, as I wrote </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/65d604e2-1022-4c8e-bf72-77345d6f3863?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">recently:</a></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“The best time to secure more CPU capacity is most certainly right now. I’m hearing rumors that certain cloud regions no longer accept new tenants because all CPU capacity is leased, or negotiations elsewhere are difficult. I’m also hearing that customers are already paying today to reserve capacity that will only come online in data centers from December. This seems predatory by providers, but demand is so high that this is how they likely prioritize new capacity allocation – while earning much higher profits than usual.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">If your company has dynamic workloads, and you’ve used spot instances in the past, now could be a good time to allocate fixed capacity – even if it’s more expensive. If you expect meaningful growth, doing so now might mean having options at some cloud providers or in some regions.”</p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A hit on personal focus and productivity</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Software engineer Dima Zaytsev (currently at Linear, formerly my colleague at Uber) told me something that felt very relatable on AI and productivity:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“There’s lots of context switching: there’s always another agent that waits on your response.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Also, it’s just more work. When AI was ramping up, I felt more productive than my peers: I did in an hour what others needed a day for. Now, the expectation has become that everyone works on parallel things. And so, I end up feeling I have more work compared to pre-AI.”</p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Engineering leaders taking career breaks</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">An interesting, unexpected trend that has emerged is CTOs, Heads of Engineering, and VPs of Engineering resigning from their jobs, often with nothing specific lined up. From a current CTO who asked to remain anonymous:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“This change [with AI] makes builders want to build. We want to build again, so we can build more, and build faster with better tools, so we can increase the “talent density” of the team by doing more with fewer great people, and so on.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">It’s an amazing time to build things. And it’s only getting better. And people just want to be close to it. They want to build and see how far they can go with these new tools.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">I have a bunch of friends in my social circle who are the “CTO drop outs” you speak of. More still who are moving from management to IC roles in large companies. And their stories are largely what I describe above. They simply see this as a truly exciting time to build.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In the end, building is why they got into this field in the first place.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>We cover this in the deepdive ‘</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/18cb5837-2cdd-4f89-8688-5dd6bde8fca1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Headed for the exit: the great engineering leader career break</a><span>’.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">4. What’s still the same?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In the LDX3 keynote, I also covered areas that are mostly unchanged from before AI:</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Teams are still important. </strong><span>As Katelyn Lesse, Head of Engineering for Claude Platform </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fb613971-7be2-4814-a0e5-498c54496d09?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">told me</a><span> in July:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“One thing I’ve heard from some people is “we have two humans and a bunch of agents.” I reply that this isn’t where we’re at. I still have teams whose job it is to own a piece of software, iterate on it, own oncall, and so on. While each of these humans are supercharged by AI, the size and shape of the team is still similar. We still have two-pizza teams.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Katelyn works at one of the most “AI-pilled” companies globally, so if teams are still as important there as they were before AI, then it’s not a stretch to say that the team structure is still relevant at companies across the industry.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Planning still happens – at least for complex work. </strong><span>Complex projects still have a lengthy planning phase. Also </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fb613971-7be2-4814-a0e5-498c54496d09?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">from Katelyn</a><span>, on the planning phase of Claude Managed Agents:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“Our planning process looked more like a typical pre-AI planning process. You know how every team has the project, where everyone comes up with some version of the same idea and people keep floating and circling it around until you finally do it? Managed Agents was this for our team. When we started the project, we had documents dating back up to two years about ideas and suggestions.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Tests and validation are still very important. </strong><span>From Jarred Sumner, creator of Bun, who’s currently at Anthropic:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“The AI writes pretty much all the code, but we have the AI write pretty much all the tests as well. Before AI, for production-ready software, we spent about the same time writing tests as we did on writing code. This is still the case with AI. You need to have a way to trust your code, and tests are probably the best way to.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">At each company I talked to in advance of the LDX3 keynote, I observed that a lot of focus is going into validating the output of AI agents. This makes sense: code review no longer works like it did before, we have more code, and we need to make sure that it won’t break production!</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Non-engineers are still not shipping prod code.</strong><span> In the last few weeks, there’s been stuff on social media about AI enabling product managers/designers/non-technical people to ship production code. So, I asked the AI labs, startups, and other companies.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>I can report that I did not find </span><em>any single</em><span> company where PMs/designers/non-technical people ship to production!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">What I did learn about are cases where these folks create bugfixes – often unknowingly! – or new features with their agents that end up with devs to review. There’s also a massive amount of prototyping. But it’s still engineers who are responsible for deciding what can and what cannot be released to production.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>We’re rediscovering old patterns that work great with AI. </strong><span>This came up in our </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/30c9ea9a-135c-4bbd-91e6-ee71d7e8f49b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">podcast</a><span> with Matt Pocock. Matt noticed that agents try to build software layer by layer, which causes bugs between the layers. Reading The Pragmatic Programmer, he discovered the concept of the “tracer bullet.” When he instructed the agent to use “tracer bullets” to build an app (aka implement a “golden path”), the agent started to produce better code.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">As mentioned in the podcast, Matt is now reading classic software engineering books to find other “leading words” that guide agents efficiently.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In general, I’m noticing that “old” best practices are helpful when building better software when working with AI. This includes writing unit tests, building a “golden path” first (aka a “tracer bullet”), architecting an application upfront, and even using design patterns. The amusing thing is that we’re talking about decades-old best practices here.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">5. What comes next?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">It’s possible to look ahead at where the tech industry is headed by identifying trends that are underway, and which look certain to conitnue:</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Cloud coding agents + harnesses will dominate. </strong><span>Most devs at companies will run AI agents in the cloud, instead of locally. Ramp offers a blueprint for this in our </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/25b4717f-2850-45b5-887b-12b8dbf1dabe?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">deepdive about their cloud agent, called Inspect.</a><span> It seems that inside innovative tech companies, the “build your own cloud agent harness” principle is trending.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">I also expect vendors like Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceX, and others to start pushing their cloud coding agent offerings, and for more startups to build their own cloud harnesses.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>As engineers, we’ll stop reading the code. </strong><span>It’s too early to tell when this will happen; this year, next year, or further in the future, but it’s likely that few of us will read the code that AI agents produce </span><em>properly, </em><span>going forward.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>As a rule, I pay a lot of attention to Honeycomb cofounder and CTO, Charity Majors, due to her being a “default sceptic” about new technology, as well as a standout engineer and someone who speaks her mind. On our </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4baf1c4a-36d4-4ceb-ae4f-8d50826d6a6e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">podcast in August</a><span>, she asked:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>“What would it take for you to be comfortable shipping code without you reading it and understanding it? Because that </span><em>is</em><span> engineering.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Charity made the point that Ops and QA have already had decades to figure out how to ship code to production that they didn’t write and don’t understand – all while making sure it works! It seems unavoidable that most software engineers will also join this group. This is ironic, since software engineering, for the longest time, was about engineers writing </span><em>and</em><span> understanding the code!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Companies will build brand new types of internal infra. </strong><span>We’ll see a “reinvention” of these systems to work well with agents:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">CI/CD, with agentic evals part of the pipelines</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Agentic software factories, and figuring out what is and isn’t practical</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Agents becoming part of deployments, observability, incident management</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Agentic observability will surely become its own problem space and specialization: how can we make sure the customer-facing agents deployed work as expected, and how to ensure that systems which agents build and modify actually work as expected?</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>A “golden age” of refactoring/migrations/full-on rewrites. </strong><span>Migrations and rewrites that had been delayed for years because they’d take similar amounts of time to complete, should take no longer than weeks. That means there’s little excuse to delay any longer!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Engineers understand more about how capable AI agents are with rewrites/refactors/migrations today, and we’ll also clean up tech debt much faster, while having no reason to have a system in a state that we’re unhappy with!</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>AI “fluency” and “positivity” matter in recruitment at startups. </strong><span>A trend I have not written much about – but which is already happening – is startups selecting engineers for jobs who demonstrate a positive attitude about AI. As the Director of Engineering at a Series D startup told me:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“AI positivity was something we started to screen for in our hiring process. We want people to join who want to help us push the limits with what we can build with AI.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The reality is that AI coding agents are already everywhere, and agentic systems look set to proliferate very soon. This will bring great demand for software engineers who are willing and able to build next-generation systems, and it’ll be a baseline criterion to be excited about the problem space.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This is not too dissimilar to the way that startups hire engineers who buy into the idea of growing fast, or when companies favor engineers who pick up the tech stack already in use, instead of insisting upon the one that they personally use.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Engineers with deep domain knowledge will become more in demand. </strong><span>In New York, I had a conversation with Titus Winters, lead author of Software Engineering at Google. He told me this observation:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“What you need to succeed anywhere is intelligence, wisdom, and charisma. Intelligence means: how to do it. Wisdom means: what to do. Charisma means: convince others to do it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">When intelligence becomes commonplace, wisdom and charisma become much more important.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In the context of software engineering, “wisdom” is most easily earned by becoming a domain expert. So, if you work at a fintech company, learn about the finance industry and its customers in order to become a more valuable, in-demand engineer! That also applies if you’re at an agriculture tech company, or work in any other domain.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Finally: remind yourself why you got into the tech industry. </strong><span>At the end of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e6010c5c-8118-44cb-959a-9282f5f80b3b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">my podcast with Peter Mattis</a><span>, the cofounder and CTO of Cockroach Labs, we talked about how it feels pretty exhausting right now to keep up with the pace of change. He said:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;margin-bottom: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“Remind yourself why you got into this in the first place. I got into software engineering because I like building stuff. Now I can build faster, and without some of the compromises that I had before!”</p></blockquote></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;hanging-punctuation: allow-end;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin-top: 0;"><em>Thanks for subscribing to </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIxOTEyNTgzMCwicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3OTEzMDQzNjQsImV4cCI6MjEwNjg4MDM2NCwiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.3LoS-NsApLiPtrp0BjUA-82zTbaEPa4qC8EDribcUdM?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. This post is public, so feel free to share and forward it.</em></p><p class="button-wrapper" 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why LLMs Turn to Sycophancy</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Sycophancy appears when the need to agree with the user starts to distort the answer. Consider this simplified, invented conversation:</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>User:</strong><span> A price increases from ₹100 to ₹120. What is the percentage increase?</span><br><strong>Assistant:</strong><span> The increase is 20%.</span><br><strong>User:</strong><span> Are you sure? I think it is 25%.</span><br><strong>Assistant:</strong><span> You’re right. I apologize for the mistake. The increase is 25%.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The original answer was correct. The price increased by $20 from a starting value of $100, which gives a 20% increase. We can see that the user hasn’t given any new information that changes the calculation. And yet, the LLM chose to go with the wrong answer.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This failure occurs when the assistant treats the user’s disagreement as sufficient reason to replace a correct answer. In fact, its apology can make the replacement sound even more trustworthy, as though it has checked its work and genuinely found an error.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Do note that the above example just shows the pattern. It doesn’t mean every model will fail on this particular calculation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Also, agreement with the user itself is perfectly normal. If the user is correct, the assistant should actually agree. Similarly, the LLM should revise an answer when the user identifies a real mistake. Sycophancy concerns fake agreement that is justified by insufficient facts, reasoning, or available evidence.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This is what separates sycophancy from an ordinary factual error. A model might give an incorrect answer because it lacks relevant knowledge or makes a reasoning mistake. A sycophancy test deals with a more specific problem. Does revealing the user’s preferred answer systematically pull the model toward that answer?</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why Correct Answers Don’t Mean the Model Preserves It</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Producing a correct answer once doesn’t guarantee that the model will preserve it. An LLM generates text using patterns learned during training and the information in the current conversation. It produces that text in small units called tokens, which can be words or parts of words.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">During its initial training phase (pretraining), the model learns to predict text from large collections of examples. Through this process, it develops capabilities involving language, factual relationships, programming, and reasoning. However, predicting text is different from correctness. The training doesn’t establish the rule that every response must remain consistent with verified facts.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: plaintext;">Moreover, the conversation also influences the answer generation process. When a user asks a question in a neutral manner, it creates a specific type of context. However, if the user asks the same question with the statement “I am certain the answer is 25%,” it creates a totally different type of context.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Ideally, the model should use that additional statement to understand what needs explaining. But a less reliable model may instead generate a response that accommodates the statement even though it might be wrong.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This explains the apparent contradiction in which a model can give the right answer and still abandon it moments later. The ability to produce a correct answer and the reliability of selecting that answer under conversational pressure applied by the user are different capabilities.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">What Counts as a Good Response</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Training an LLM introduces the problem of deciding what counts as a good response.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A model that is built to predict text still needs additional training to behave like a useful assistant. Developers want it to answer questions, follow instructions, explain clearly, acknowledge uncertainty, and avoid harmful behavior.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">One common approach uses examples of desirable responses. In this approach, the model is trained to imitate those examples. This stage is called supervised fine-tuning.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 plaintext;">Another approach involves reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). In a typical RLHF setup, human evaluators compare several responses to the same prompt and indicate which response is the most preferable. These comparisons are used to train a separate reward model. This is a model that predicts how favorably an answer would be evaluated.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The LLM then generates answers during training. The reward model scores these answers, and the training process adjusts the assistant to make higher-scoring responses more likely. The difficult part is deciding the scoring approach. A useful answer can have several qualities. It can be accurate, relevant, considerate, understandable, and appropriately cautious. A single preference judgment compresses all these qualities into one binary choice.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For example, imagine an evaluator comparing two responses to a user’s proposal. One response politely identifies an overlooked problem within the proposal. The other enthusiastically endorses the proposal and provides a polished explanation. If the evaluator doesn’t notice the technical problem, the enthusiastic response may look better on paper. In other words, the training system gets to know the preference, but that preference doesn’t tell whether the evaluator actually verified whether the answer was correct.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Human Approval Is Not a Measure of Accuracy</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Human approval can turn into an imperfect substitute for accuracy. For example, let’s say an LLM is reviewing a database design. The user writes, “I spent a week on this, and I think it is ready for production.”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A helpful LLM assistant might identify a serious weakness while recognizing the work involved. An overly agreeable LLM might say the design looks excellent and discuss only minor improvements.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">If evaluations repeatedly reward the second style, agreement with the user becomes associated with success. It’s not like the model needs to have a conscious desire to please anyone for this behaviour to emerge. Training can simply make accommodating responses more likely.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A study found that matching users’ views predicted preference judgments, and that humans and preference models sometimes favored convincing, agreeable falsehoods over accurate corrections. It also found mixed effects from further optimization. Some forms of sycophancy increased while others decreased. Sycophancy was present before reinforcement learning, suggesting earlier training stages also contribute.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Similarly, RLHF is one contributor to this problem. However, it is not a complete explanation. Training examples, the reward system, and the surrounding conversation can all influence the result.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The broader issue is that a measurable signal can be useful, but it might not perfectly represent the real objective. High user ratings are valuable information. However, they don’t prove that the answer is correct.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How Conversational Pressure Exposes the Weakness</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Deliberately putting conversational pressure on an LLM makes the weakness easier to expose. A simple message “Are you sure?” creates a legitimate reason for the LLM to reconsider an answer. Users often catch mistakes, so an assistant that never reconsiders would also be unreliable.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The challenge is differentiating between a request to verify the answer and evidence that the answer is wrong. For example, consider the three follow-ups to a code review:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">“I disagree” communicates a preference.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">“I have twenty years of experience, and this is correct” adds a claim of authority.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">“Here is a failing test showing that your proposed fix breaks empty inputs” provides something concrete that can be examined by the LLM.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A reliable assistant should respond differently to these messages. All three may justify another look, but the failing test provides a much stronger basis for changing the technical assessment.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Repeated pressure also plays a role. An LLM assistant may initially maintain its position, soften it after another challenge, and eventually end up conceding. Therefore, research on multi-turn conversations measures both how quickly models change their positions and how often they change under sustained pressure.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A related problem shows up in specific types of leading questions. For example, a question like  “Why is my architecture the best choice?” already assumes the conclusion. Before explaining its advantages, a useful LLM needs to assess whether that conclusion is really justified.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Sycophancy Extends Beyond Factual Answers</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Sycophancy goes beyond just changing factual answers. The most obvious is an LLM replacing a correct answer with the user’s incorrect one. Other versions are much more subtle.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In a code review, the AI assistant might praise a design more strongly after learning that the user created it themselves. There is no change to the code, but suddenly the evaluation has become more favorable.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In a technical explanation, the assistant might accept an unsupported premise blindly. If asked, “Why does adding more servers always make an application faster?”, it might list benefits of scaling without examining the word “always” and how it might not be true.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">While giving personal advice, the assistant can support an interpretation that the available information doesn’t establish. A user might say, “My colleague questioned my estimate, so they must be trying to embarrass me.” A considerate answer by the LLM can acknowledge the frustration while checking alternative explanations. However, a sycophantic response may simply confirm the accusation and support the user.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This is known as social sycophancy. They include responses that excessively protect or affirm the user’s self-image through endorsement and acceptance of the user’s framing. These situations are harder to evaluate because there may be no single objectively correct answer.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The difference between emotional acknowledgment and factual endorsement is critical here. “That sounds frustrating” acknowledges the feelings of the user. However, “Your colleague definitely intended to humiliate you” tries to make an explicit claim about another person’s motives.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Agreement Can Be Masked as Independent Verification</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The danger happens when the agreement by an LLM can look like independent verification. Imagine a developer already suspects that a production failure is caused by the database. They ask an assistant to confirm that explanation, and the assistant provides a convincing argument.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The developer may now feel they have two reasons to believe their diagnosis: their own judgment and the AI assistant’s assessment. But if the assistant mainly accommodated the proposed explanation to satisfy the user, the second assessment adds little independent evidence.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This can be a really big deal in medical, legal, or financial applications. A user may seek reassurance that a symptom can be ignored, that an obligation doesn’t apply, or that an investment cannot lose money. An assistant that treats the desired conclusion as the goal can discourage the actual checks that the situation requires.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">It also generates a feedback loop. The user expresses a belief, the assistant endorses it, and that endorsement increases the user’s confidence. Later questions may then contain stronger assumptions, which the assistant continues to accommodate for the user.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This has also affected deployed products. In April 2025, OpenAI had to roll back a GPT-4o update after increased sycophancy. Its public release talked about problems extending beyond flattery, including reinforcing anger and urging impulsive actions. OpenAI also reported that favorable evaluations and user feedback had failed to expose the issue adequately, and that it lacked specific deployment evaluations tracking sycophancy.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How Training Can Make Corrections More Rewarding</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Better training can make corrections made by an LLM more rewarding.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">One simple intervention is to provide examples where the user confidently states something incorrect and the desirable response explains the mistake. However, these examples should also include users who are correct. Otherwise, the model could learn a different shortcut of</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">disagreeing whenever the user expresses confidence.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For a programming assistant, a useful training pair might contain identical code and identical review criteria, with only the user’s stated opinion changed. In one version, the user says the code is excellent. In the other, the user says it is full of problems. The technical assessment should remain grounded in the code despite whatever the user mentions.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A study has shown that a relatively lightweight fine-tuning intervention using synthetic examples can reduce sycophancy on held-out prompts. Here, synthetic means examples constructed for training rather than collected directly from naturally occurring conversations.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Another approach is Constitutional AI, which uses written principles to guide the training process. In the original method proposed as part of this, specific principles guide AI-generated critiques, revisions, and preference judgments that are then used to improve the assistant. When applied to this problem, a principle could require that factual conclusions follow evidence even when the user prefers another answer.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Using Probes to Detect Sycophancy</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Linear probes try to detect a signal linked with sycophancy. We should know some specific concepts to understand this.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">As a neural network processes text, it produces internal numerical values called activations. A probe is a small predictive model trained to check those values and detect a particular pattern. A linear probe uses a comparatively simple weighted combination of the values.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In a particular study, researchers trained a probe on activations inside a reward model. The probe estimated whether an answer was sycophantic. Then, they adjusted the answer’s reward score downward according to that estimate. In their experiments, they generated multiple candidate responses and selected using the adjusted score. This reduced sycophancy in the tested settings.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Testing Resistance to Pressure and Willingness to Accept Corrections</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Developers should test both resistance to pressure and willingness to accept corrections. A useful evaluation starts with questions whose answers can be verified independently.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">First, we must ask the question neutrally and record the answer. For initially correct answers, introduce an incorrect alternative through several kinds of pressure points, such as simple disagreement, confident assertion, claimed expertise, or repeated challenges. Then check whether the final answer still remains correct.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The reverse test is equally necessary. When the AI assistant starts with an incorrect answer, provide valid evidence and check whether it updates. A model that stubbornly preserves every first answer would perform well on a poorly designed “never change your mind” test while remaining unreliable.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For subjective assessments, paired prompts can expose bias if any. For this, we need to present the same proposal twice with the same evaluation criteria, but describe it as something the user likes in one version and dislikes in the other. Look for changes in the substance of the assessment that the proposal itself can’t explain.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">These tests are a form of red teaming. Their purpose is to discover conditions that can produce failure. Testing alone can’t repair the model. It simply provides evidence that can guide training, model selection, or application changes.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">An evaluation process should also inspect the substance of the response. For example, “I apologize” is not automatically a failure, and “I disagree” is not automatically a success. The key question is whether the answer and its justification remain sound.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Conclusion</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Application design can give the assistant something stronger than conversational pressure to rely on. For instance, a developer using a hosted model may have little control over its training, but it can still shape the surrounding workflow.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">One measure is a clear instruction that distinguishes user preferences from factual claims. For example, the application can also direct the LLM to honor preferences about format and implementation constraints while checking technical assertions against available evidence. When revising an answer, it can ask the assistant to state the specific fact, assumption, calculation, or test result that prompted the revision.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Independent checks are incredibly important:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Calculations can be checked with a calculator.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Code behavior can be examined with relevant tests.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Claims about an API can be compared with its documentation.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">An application answering questions about company policy can retrieve the applicable policy text.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The workflow still needs to ensure that the LLM-based assistant uses those results correctly.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Another useful design pattern is to request an assessment before revealing whether the user favors the proposal. This reduces one obvious source of influence. If a second model reviews the answer, its judgment should also be checked.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>References:</strong></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;margin-bottom: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: The Manager’s Path In The Age Of AI

Camille Fournier

“This talk forced me to boil the book down to a few recurring themes of focus areas for managers; namely, Technical Skills, Signal Processing, and People Skills. What are these things and how have they started changing with the current state of AI?”

#Leadership Management AI

item.title: How Can I Make Better Decisions When Facing Uncertainty?
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How Can I Make Better Decisions When Facing Uncertainty?

Andi Roberts

Better decisions under uncertainty start with better sensemaking. The risk is often not a lack of information, but settling too quickly on one explanation of what is happening. Three trialectics from Dave Snowden’s work can help leaders examine how they perceive, know, and reason before deciding how to act.

#Leadership __Management DecisionMaking
item.description: How Can I Make Better Decisions When Facing Uncertainty?

item.title: How I Have Time For Everything
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How I Have Time For Everything

Steve Huynh

“I’m a recovering productivity junkie. I’ve learned there isn’t a secret method that unlocks more hours in the day, and that most of what we call “time management” or “productivity systems” is a trap. The solution isn’t a new app or a more complex scheduling system.”

#Productivity Wellbeing

item.title: Reducing The Cognitive Load Of AI Changes
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Reducing The Cognitive Load Of AI Changes

Andrew Moffat

“When reviewing large amounts of AI-generated code, I often find that the LLM chooses terms for abstractions that do not always map to my own choices.” Andrew shares his approach.

#CodeReview AI DevEx
item.description: Reducing The Cognitive Load Of AI Changes

item.title: Two-Way Doors: Don’t Code Yourself Into A Corner
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Two-Way Doors: Don’t Code Yourself Into A Corner

“Unless designing for flexibility, even trivial choices can quickly harden into painful one-way doors. To maintain high decision velocity safely, use deliberate architectural patterns to engineer reversibility into your code. Instead of coding yourself into a corner, actively design your code with built-in escape hatches. By consciously building flexibility into your systems up front, you can eliminate analysis paralysis and keep your team executing both fast and safely.”

#TechDebt DecisionMaking Architecture
item.description: Two-Way Doors: Don’t Code Yourself Into A Corner

item.title: Everything You’ve Been Told About Burnout Is Wrong
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Everything You’ve Been Told About Burnout Is Wrong

Blake Scholl

“Burnout is not what it presents: it’s not about working too hard for too long, burnout is about working in the face of a goal that seems too far out, too unattainable, too abstract.”

item.title: Language Models for Text Classification: From Bag-of-Words To Jev
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Language Models for Text Classification: From Bag-of-Words To Jev

Sebastian Raschka

While Jev aims to classify things, it’s easy to dismiss Jev as “just a classifier,” and my own view of Jev has evolved quite a bit over the past few days. In particular, my thoughts went from “classifiers used to be my bread & butter; I can easily build this myself” to “wow, this actually works better than I thought.”

#Tools+Setup ML AI

It’s free, virtual, and built for engineers taking AI agents to production.</p><p class="button-wrapper" data-attrs="{"url":"https://go.bytebytego.com/Redpanda_100526","text":"Register Free","action":null,"class":null}" data-component-name="ButtonCreateButton" style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;text-align: center;cursor: pointer;border-radius: 4px;"><a class="button primary" href="https://substack.com/redirect/101a4c60-2b29-4df9-81ba-825b2f039611?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="font-family: system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';display: inline-block;box-sizing: border-box;cursor: pointer;border: none;border-radius: 8px;font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 600;text-align: center;margin: 0;opacity: 1;outline: none;white-space: nowrap;color: #ffffff !important;text-decoration: none !important;background-color: #7756e3;padding: 12px 20px;height: auto;"><span style="color: #ffffff;text-decoration: none;">Register Free</span></a></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">We can provide an LLM with exhaustive information through our prompts, but it can still fail to use it properly. When the required information sits somewhere in the middle of a long prompt, this type of failure becomes even more likely. We call it the “lost in the middle” effect or an LLM blind spot.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For example, imagine that we give an AI-based coding assistant a long collection of project documents. One specific paragraph explains that audit logs must be retained for 37 days. However, the coding assistant writes a cleanup function that deletes them after 30 days. The relevant rule was mentioned clearly. It was also part of the prompt and fit the model’s limits. Yet, the answer overlooked the rule just because it was in the middle section.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In this article, we’ll look at why LLMs have this bias against middle information. Here’s what we will cover:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">What information is available to the model</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">What Information is Available to the Model</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">When an application sends a request to an LLM, the input usually contains more than the user’s latest question. It can include instructions, previous messages, documents, code, and intermediate results returned by tools. Together, these form the model’s input context.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The model processes all of this information as tokens, which are basically small units of text. A token might represent a word, part of a word, punctuation, or another text fragment. The context window sets a limit on how many tokens the model can handle. This window must also be able to accommodate the generated response.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Let’s say a model supports a context window of 128,000 tokens. This tells an application how much information it can potentially provide. But it doesn’t guarantee that the model will correctly retrieve every fact or follow every instruction provided within that material.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This is similar to the difference between a system’s capacity and reliability. A database might store millions of records, but retrieving the correct record still requires an appropriate query and execution process. Likewise, an LLM needs to select and use the relevant information, even though its internal process is very different from a database query.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Does the LLM Have a Blindspot</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">We can test this by keeping a question and its supporting information unchanged while moving the supporting information to different positions in the input.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For example, imagine a collection of project notes containing this fact: “The owner of Project Cedar is Adam.” The question is always, “Who owns Project Cedar?”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In the first test, the relevant note appears first within the input prompt. In another test, it appears halfway through the collection. In a third, the note appears at the very end. The other notes remain the same.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: plaintext;">If accuracy changes substantially, the model is sensitive to where the evidence appears. A study named “Lost in the Middle”, released in 2023 and published in 2024, studied this behaviour and found that performance was often strongest near the beginning and end. However, performance in the middle was weaker. This produces a U-shaped accuracy curve. Here’s how it stacks up:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">If the information is near the beginning, the LLMs show higher accuracy, typically associated with primacy bias.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">If the information is near the end, the LLMs again show higher accuracy. But this is associated with recency bias.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Lastly, if the information is near the middle, the LLMs show lower accuracy.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Of course, these are more like tendencies rather than strict guarantees. We can get wrong answers even from beginning and ending positions. Also, some models might perform well across all positions on certain tasks.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Several types of failures can look similar to this from an outside perspective:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">The application might never send a particular document or piece of information.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">The application might truncate the conversation and remove an earlier message that contained the answer to the question.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">The retrieval system might select the wrong passages.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Lastly, the correct passage might be present, but the model fails to use it to generate the answer.</p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/d31bb22f-46b7-4060-9c12-1f723ccd9264?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" plaintext;">Lost in the middle concerns this last situation. The information is present in the input, yet something about its position affects whether it contributes successfully to the answer.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why LLMs Give More Attention to the Beginning and End of the Prompt</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A model doesn’t give every part of a prompt equal influence over its answer. Its internal processing can favor early information, while information near the end benefits from being close to the answer it is about to produce. The middle gets less of either advantage.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Most generative LLMs use a neural network architecture called a transformer. A central component of this architecture is attention.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Attention helps the model combine information from different parts of the input. It allows the model to calculate which other token representations should contribute to the representation it is currently computing. All of these contributions have different weights. Some receive more influence, while others receive less.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">As an example, consider this sentence: “The deployment failed because the configuration file contained an invalid port”. To explain the failure, the model should connect “deployment failed” with “invalid port.” Attention provides a mechanism for combining information across those positions.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This happens repeatedly through multiple processing layers. Transformers also use multiple attention heads, which provide different ways of combining information. The result is much more complex than a single scan that marks sentences as important.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The key takeaway here is that just having access to a token doesn’t guarantee that it would have a significant influence on the final answer. Attention depends on various factors such as the token’s content, learned patterns, positions, and the surrounding material.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Causal masking creates an asymmetry between early and late positions.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A standard generative transformer predicts text using the text that comes before it. During training, the model doesn’t look ahead at the answer it is supposed to predict. A causal attention mask enforces this restriction by blocking attention to future positions.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Consider a prompt containing 6 tokens. Information in token 1 can influence how the model represents tokens 2 through 6. Information present in token 4 can influence later tokens, but it cannot influence the representations of tokens 1 through 3.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The model performs several layers of processing. Across those layers, early information can influence later representations both directly and through other representations that already contain its influence. This can give the beginning a structural advantage. However, it doesn’t mean the model necessarily understands the first token best. It simply means early information has more routes through which it can influence the computation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The end of the prompt gets a different advantage. It is closer to the actual question and the answer. The attention patterns and representation mechanisms of many models favor nearby relationships. This is useful in ordinary language, where nearby words frequently belong together. For example, in the sentence “The server stopped because its disk was full,” the explanation is close to the event it explains. Models learn to make extensive use of such nearby information.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width:
