auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">When a question comes after a long document, the final paragraphs are nearby, while the middle paragraphs are much farther away. Depending on the model, those nearby paragraphs can be easier to use.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">However, there are two important qualifications to the simplified “token 1 accumulates massive attention” explanation:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">First, permission to attend doesn’t determine the actual attention weight given to a token. The model doesn’t maintain one continuously accumulating importance score for each token.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Second, when generating an answer after the prompt, standard full causal attention can access all earlier prompt positions, including the middle.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Therefore, the middle is not directly hidden from the answer by the causal mask. The issue involves how information is represented and combined throughout the network.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why Larger Context Windows Cannot Solve the Problem</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Larger context windows are great at increasing the overall capacity of a model. But they don’t guarantee uniform reliability when it comes to making every position equally useful.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">We can distinguish between the two in terms of maximum context size and effective context size for a task. The first concerns the overall supported input size. The second concerns how much context the application can actually use while maintaining acceptable performance.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Effective context size depends on the task. For example, the task of finding one distinctive identifier within some documents is different from comparing several documents, resolving contradictions, or tracking changes across a long conversation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This is where the RULER benchmark becomes relevant. The original benchmark evaluated 17 models using tasks that went beyond simple retrieval, including following chains of information and aggregating results. It found widespread degradation as input length increased. However, its limitations explicitly state that it reported scores by input length without controlling for and reporting evidence position.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Strategies to Mitigate the Bias</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">While it is difficult to completely remove the bias against middle information from a model, there are a few strategies that we can use to mitigate it.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" plaintext;">Let’s look at them in more detail:</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Prompt Optimization</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Prompt organization helps make important material easier to use. A good starting point is to make the task, essential constraints, and final questions easy to identify for the model. We should not bury important information inside a large block of unrelated material.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For a coding task, a short opening statement might clearly mention a compatibility requirement. The relevant source files can follow, with a precise request at the end. For document question answering, putting the question after the documents is another useful arrangement to test.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Clear boundaries to mark different types of content also help. Markdown headings, document labels, and XML-style tags can distinguish instructions from source material and separate one document from another. However, these are practical starting points whose effectiveness should be checked on the chosen model.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For example, an application could assemble a prompt like this:</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><pre class="shiki github-light" tabindex="0" style="background-color: rgb(250,250,250);padding: 20px;margin-top: 0;margin-bottom: 20px;outline: 1px solid rgb(0,0,0,.1);outline-offset: -1px;border-radius: 8px;box-sizing: border-box;font-family: ui-monospace,SFMono-Regular,'SF Mono',Menlo,Consolas,'Liberation Mono',monospace;font-size: 13px;line-height: 20px;color: #24292e"><code><span class="line"><span>Task: Propose a change to the cleanup worker.</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Critical constraint: Audit logs must remain available for 37 days.</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span><document id="retention-policy"></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Audit logs must be retained for 37 days.</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></document></span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span><document id="cleanup-worker"></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>[Relevant implementation]</span></span>
<span class="line"><span></document></span></span>
<span class="line"><span></span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Request:</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Identify the required retention period and its source.</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Then propose the code change.</span></span>
<span class="line"><span>Check that the change preserves the retention requirement.</span></span></code></pre></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Here, the constraint comes from the supplied source. The documents have distinct identities, and the final request specifies what evidence the answer must use.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Adding these tags doesn’t change the model’s attention mask or guarantee compliance. Their main purpose is to reduce ambiguity about the organization of the input. Brief repetition can also help keep a crucial constraint visible. However, repeating the entire prompt several times adds length and can introduce contradictions if the copies diverge.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Pruning Unnecessary Context</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">It is much more useful to reduce unnecessary context than enforcing an arbitrary token limit.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For example, model providers would often advise staying below a certain number of tokens, such as 20K tokens. This is more of an application-specific budget rather than a scientific boundary. There is no universal threshold at which 19,999 tokens are reliable and 20,001 become unreliable. A short prompt can fail if its instructions conflict. On the other hand, a much longer prompt can succeed when the evidence is clear, and the task is straightforward.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>A better approach is to add the information needed for the task while removing material that adds little value. We should select relevant information and manage context as an application resource.</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d3438bac-460a-4b14-ad9b-875ae967eebd?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: #7756e3;text-decoration: none;"> </a><span>Let’s say an AI assistant is investigating a database connection error. Supplying months of logs, every configuration file, and an entire deployment history creates considerable unnecessary material. A more focused input might contain the error, the relevant connection settings, the affected code, and recent changes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">As you can notice, the main difficulty is deciding what is unnecessary. If we remove an exception, dependency, or earlier decision, it will make the prompt shorter but also make it less accurate. Therefore, context selection needs to preserve the evidence required to answer the question while removing useless information.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The same care should be applied to long conversations. An application can maintain a concise record of current requirements and decisions, with references back to the original material. Summaries are useful, but they can omit details, so they should not become the only surviving source when exact information matters.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Retrieval with RAG</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Retrieval can reduce the amount of searching the model must perform inside its prompt.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A retrieval system searches a larger collection and selects relevant material before the LLM answers. This approach is commonly called retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Consider an AI-based support application with thousands of documentation pages. For a question about webhook retries, the system could retrieve the retry policy, relevant configuration documentation, and applicable exceptions. The LLM then answers from that smaller collection.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Retrieval can use keyword search, database queries, semantic search, or combinations of these methods. The key change is that the application takes responsibility for finding likely evidence instead of always placing the entire collection in the prompt and hoping for the best.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">To be clear, this approach also has its own problems. The retrieval search may still miss the relevant passage. A retrieved excerpt may omit a necessary exception. Retrieving too many passages may recreate the original problem.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For that reason, RAG doesn’t eliminate “lost in the middle”. The retrieved material still needs sensible selection, ordering, and evaluation.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Conclusion</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The lost-in-the-middle problem reveals a blind spot for LLMs. Availability of information doesn’t guarantee that it will be used effectively. A fact can remain inside the context window and still contribute very little to the answer. What looks like forgetting is often a quirk of the attention mechanism to give relevant information enough influence during generation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This happens partly because different positions can receive different advantages. Early information has more opportunities to influence later processing, while information near the end can benefit from its proximity to the question and the answer. Information in the middle does not benefit from both. However, the strength of this effect varies with the model, its training, and the task.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin-bottom: 0;">We can try to have a larger context window to expand capacity, but reliable use of that capacity still needs testing. Clear instructions, well-organized source material, and careful placement of essential details can help generate better results. Removing unnecessary context and retrieving relevant passages can also make the task easier, provided important details and exceptions are preserved. These techniques reduce the chances of overlooking information. But they don’t guarantee perfect answers.</p></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><table item.title: Last time my family was replaced by technology
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Last time my family was replaced by technology

Manuel Darcemont

2 minutes by Manuel Darcemont Manuel shares a family story about a French farrier who became a mechanic when cars arrived reframes today's fears about AI replacing developers. Past generations faced the same dread when tractors and engines upended their trades. What carried them through was holding onto their purpose rather than their tools. If what drives you is building things and solving problems, that purpose can survive a change in how you do it.
item.description: Last time my family was replaced by technology

item.title: Making your own dithered QR codes
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Making your own dithered QR codes

Andrew Taylor

5 minutes by Andrew Taylor QR codes store data in a grid of squares, where some squares help scanners locate the code and others store the actual data. By shrinking the data squares and filling the space with image pixels, you can embed a photo into a QR code. Error diffusion dithering improves image quality and hides noise caused by data squares. Prettier codes scan less reliably though, so consider where and how the code will be used.
item.description: Making your own dithered QR codes

item.title: Railway-oriented programming
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Railway-oriented programming

Sunhyoup Lee

22 minutes by Sunhyoup Lee Errors and side effects are unavoidable in software, but there are structured ways to handle them. Two common approaches are checking conditions before acting or catching exceptions after the fact. Railway-Oriented Programming takes a different route, using functional concepts like functors and monads to split every function into a success or failure path, keeping program flow linear and predictable. It works well in many environments but is not a universal solution, and applying it everywhere can reduce readability.
item.description: Railway-oriented programming

item.title: Monolith first
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Monolith first

Martin Fowler

5 minutes by Martin Fowler Starting with microservices on a new project often leads to trouble, while successful cases usually began as monoliths first. Building a monolith early helps teams move fast, get user feedback, and find the right service boundaries before committing to a more complex structure. Once the system matures, teams can gradually split off services. Avoid microservices at the start unless your team already has solid experience with them.
item.description: Monolith first

item.title: What good is a best-effort exclusive lock, anyway?
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
What good is a best-effort exclusive lock, anyway?

Philippe Gaultier

6 minutes by Philippe Gaultier CockroachDB supports SELECT ... FOR UPDATE but treats it as best-effort under its default SERIALIZABLE isolation. Unlike Postgres, it does not guarantee exclusive row locking. Instead, it uses fast in-memory locks to reduce contention by making competing transactions wait their turn. Correctness still comes from SERIALIZABLE itself, which ensures only one conflicting transaction commits while others retry. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: What good is a best-effort exclusive lock, anyway?

item.title: What is middleware in ASP.NET Core and the gotchas
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
What is middleware in ASP.NET Core and the gotchas

David Grace

Middleware in ASP.NET Core runs on every HTTP request and response. You can write it as a class, but watch out for common mistakes. Forgetting to call next stops the rest of the pipeline from running. Scoped services must be injected into InvokeAsync, not the constructor, since middleware itself lives for the whole app lifetime. You also cannot modify a response after it has started, and background tasks need their own fresh scope to avoid using disposed services.
item.description: What is middleware in ASP.NET Core and the gotchas

item.title: Beyond grep: Testing codebase memory MCP on .NET
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Beyond grep: Testing codebase memory MCP on .NET

Marek Sirkovský

Most AI coding tools waste tokens by scanning entire codebases when asked simple questions. Codebase Memory MCP tries to fix this by building a local knowledge graph of your code using tree-sitter, then exposing it to AI assistants through MCP. It works well for navigating within a single repository, but struggles with newer C# features and fails to trace relationships across repositories or NuGet package boundaries, a limitation shared by similar tools like GitNexus and Grafel.
item.description: Beyond grep: Testing codebase memory MCP on .NET

item.title: Automatic CSRF protection based on fetch metadata headers
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Automatic CSRF protection based on fetch metadata headers

Andrew Lock

Andrew takes a look at the new Cross-Site Request Forgery protection added to ASP.NET Core in .NET 11 preview 6, which relies on the Fetch Metadata HTTP headers, instead of the "traditional" anti-CSRF tokens used in earlier versions of .NET Core. He talks about CSRF attacks, the existing protections in ASP.NET Core, discusses why a new approach is possible, and provides a brief recap on Fetch Metadata headers. He also shows how this works in ASP.NET Core as of .NET 11 preview 6, and finally, he takes a look at the implementation behind the feature, as well as dives into why the new feature doesn't really help you if you're using MVC or Razor Pages.
item.description: Automatic CSRF protection based on fetch metadata headers

item.title: The hidden trap of fixed buffers in C#
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
The hidden trap of fixed buffers in C#

Kevin Gosse

Adding a constructor to a struct with a fixed buffer changes how memory is initialized. Without a constructor, the compiler zeroes all memory automatically. With one, fixed buffers are exempt from that zeroing rule, so they retain whatever values were in memory before. This is by design in the C# spec but easy to miss. The fix is to manually clear the buffer inside the constructor.
item.description: The hidden trap of fixed buffers in C#

item.title: Guid.CreateVersion7 is NOT a sequential guid for SQL server
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Guid.CreateVersion7 is NOT a sequential guid for SQL server

Bart Wullems

Using version 7 GUIDs in SQL Server causes index fragmentation, just like random GUIDs do. This happens because SQL Server sorts GUID bytes in a different order than the RFC standard, putting the timestamp in the least significant position. Bart says the fix is to let EF Core or SQL Server generate the ID, or use a library that reorders the bytes to match SQL Server's sorting rules. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: Guid.CreateVersion7 is NOT a sequential guid for SQL server

plaintext;"></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Both the machines exchange the SSH versions and negotiate crypto algorithms, and each side runs a key exchange protocol. The SSH server sends the public key and a signature, which the client machine verifies. That host key is then checked against the known_hosts file.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Both the machines then derive session keys on their end and do not share them over the network. Same keys, computed separately, never put on the wire. Then the SSH client starts authentication by sending the public key for login. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The SSH server matches the public key in the authorized_keys, and the SSH client also signs the auth request with the private key and sends the digital signature to the SSH server.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The private key never leaves your machine. The server will verify the signature with the client public key. This completes the SSH authentication, and now the session is open for communication.</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Top 6 Techniques to Make Your AI System Efficient</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Serving LLMs at scale is expensive. auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">It uses an LLM to select an action, executes that action, evaluates the result, and repeats the process until the task is complete. Let’s take a closer look at each of these components:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Brain: The LLM is the core. It reads the situation, thinks, and decides what to do next. The big shift from chatbot to agent: the model isn’t writing text anymore, it’s making choices.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><span>Planning: Hard tasks need more than one step. Agents break them down using methods like Chain of Thought (think step by step), Tree of Thoughts (try options, pick the best), or</span><br><span>Reflexion (learn from mistakes and retry). Planning turns a fuzzy goal into clear actions.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Tools: An LLM without tools is a brain in a jar. Tools are functions the model can call, like web search, code execution, APIs, files, or browsers (often using the MCP standard). The model requests a tool, the system runs it, and the result comes back.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Memory: Without memory, every turn starts from zero. Short-term memory is the context window. Long-term memory lives in vector stores, files, and knowledge bases. When the window fills up, agents summarize old turns and carry the summary forward.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Loop: All four pieces work together in a cycle. The agent looks at the current state, decides what to do, uses a tool, sees the result, and repeats. It keeps going until it gives a final answer.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Guardrails: Not strictly anatomy, but important. Sandboxing, human checks, token limits, output validation, and scope limits keep autonomy from turning into expensive chaos. The more autonomy you give, the more these matter.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Over to you: when you build an agent, which of these five takes the most work to get right?</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How do you know if your AI app actually works?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">You evaluate it. But most teams skip this step (or do it wrong) because “eval” feels vague. It’s not.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" plaintext;">Every good eval is a 3-step recipe.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Step 1: Pick a task. AI systems have different capabilities and dimensions to evaluate. For LLMs, it can be safety or math capability, in RAGs it can be grounding and retrieval, Pick one.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Step 2: Collect eval data. For every task, gather inputs paired with the right answer or expected behavior. A safety set pairs risky prompts with “refuse.”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Step 3: Develop a grader. How do you decide if the output is good?</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Use code-based graders (if/else, unit tests) for things with a clear correct answer and patch passing unit-tests.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Use model-based graders (LLM-as-judge) for subjective tasks like safety.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Use human graders for edge cases and anything where nuance matters more than throughput.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Most production evals combine all three. Code-based for what’s cheap to check. Model-based for scale. Human-based for what matters most.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Over to you: what’s the hardest thing about your task to grade, and which grader type do you use for it?</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: item.title: A Staff Engineer's Guide to Inventing Work
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
A Staff Engineer's Guide to Inventing Work

Sujith Jay Nair

“A big part of a staff engineer’s job in a platform team is to figure out what the team should build next - I like to call that “inventing work”. Thankfully, the signals that help us to invent work are already out there, and they arrive from four directions - from the systems, from the users, from your organization, and from the industry. What follows is a guide to reading each of them.”

#Strategy PlatformEngineering Staff+
item.description: A Staff Engineer's Guide to Inventing Work

item.title: How Do AI Coding Assistants Change The Shape Of Engineering Work Over Time?
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How Do AI Coding Assistants Change The Shape Of Engineering Work Over Time?

Lizzie Matusov

“Researchers at the University of Auckland surveyed professional software engineers who were very actively using using AI coding assistants during two time windows (October 2024 and April 2025). Each survey asked about time spent on six development tasks, perceived productivity, and the three DevEx dimensions, alongside open-ended questions about how the tools had changed their work.”

#Leadership AI DevEx
item.description: How Do AI Coding Assistants Change The Shape Of Engineering Work Over Time?

Hiring Breakpoints

“And there are a few important breakpoints to consider on the journey of growing your team. These might seem a bit obvious, but the important realization is that at these breakpoints hiring decisions are much more important, so if you keep them in mind as hard thresholds you’ll make better scaling decisions.”

#Management Scale Hiring

item.title: How We Made Claude 3x Faster In Two Weeks
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How We Made Claude 3x Faster In Two Weeks

“This August, we made the core user experience of Claude and the Claude desktop app about 3x faster in a two-week sprint. Users had been telling us it was slow, and they were right. We ran everything from a single Slack channel, with Claude in every thread.”

#AI CaseStudy Performance

item.title: Aho-Corasick
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Aho-Corasick

Colin James

“This post describes the construction of an Aho-Corasick automaton for the simultaneous matching of substrings within a sequence. I’m fond of this algorithm because it constructs an automaton from an existing tree data structure in a rather pleasant way.”

#DeepDive Algo

0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>TTD (time to detect): one hour? </strong><span>The Firebase team never shared how long it took them to detect that practically all iOS apps using Firebase had started to crash. On the GitHub ticket, they acknowledged the incident 70 minutes after it started</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>TTM (time to mitigate): 2-6 hours. </strong><span>It took two hours and eleven minutes to roll out the fix, but due to caching (apps that had cached the incorrect server response served this cache for additional four hours, and so kept crashing for up to six hours.)</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Incident management basics</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Firebase team itself closed the outage with a short report effectively saying that there had been an outage, but they’d resolved it now, so thanks for your patience and have a nice day.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>This handling of a high-impact incident is absolutely </span><em>not</em><span> typical of Google, the company that coined the term ‘Site Reliability Engineer’ and wrote the SRE book.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>For one, Firebase never bothered updating its status page. </strong><span>Oddly enough, the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1543495f-25dd-4077-92bc-8e87776cc14b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">official Firebase status page</a><span> showed all systems green – despite the acknowledgement of the outage. Indeed, during it and afterward, they didn’t update the status page to indicate the lengthy outage:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: reasons, including:</p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Offer transparency on the stability of the service</p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">It’s worth asking: if an outage that takes down most (or all?) iOS apps using Firebase doesn’t warrant an update to the status page, then what does!</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Will Google publish a postmortem for such a high-profile outage like this was? </strong><span>How did it happen, how did a backend change make it to production without basic validation and testing, and what’s changing so that  this category of bug doesn’t ship to production in the future?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>We would know if the Firebase team published a postmortem, but it’s unlikely this will happen. </span><em>I asked Google if they plan to do so, but got no response after two days.</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Given the customers of Firebase are all developers, it’s disappointing that Google seems unbothered about being transparent about how things went wrong and giving reassurance that they have learned from this outage in any way.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Either way, I hope Firebase audit their SDK to ensure that malformed backend data does not crash the SDK, and look through their release process so that backend changes are tested against the SDK, to avoid similar outages in the future.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: I am surprised by this approach, indicating that it would be too much effort to give basic transparency to their customers (devs!) about why the platform stopped working for hours. Maybe Google is right and it doesn’t matter any more? Nothing will happen if they don’t update their status page during an incident, nor publish a postmortem afterward?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">I’d like to think that standout incident management is where startups can do better than tech behemoths like Google and Meta, and build up the developer goodwill that Big Tech increasingly seems to not care about. As devs, we make decisions on which platforms we trust or not; platforms with no transparency or accountability after an outage feel less trustworthy to me than those that take this stuff more seriously.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">2. Use your allowance across 16 partners including Cognition’s Devin, Notion, Vercel, T3, OpenClaw, and Dactyl, and control how much each can use. Eligible OpenAI usage counts toward your plan limits. You can also sign in to a range of tools with your ChatGPT account to connect plugins faster and manage fewer passwords.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Until now, if you paid for ChatGPT or Codex – say, the $200/month plan – you have access to OpenAI’s models and Codex, and can also top up with credits to use more of OpenAI’s models. But going forward, you’ll be able to use “OpenAI credits” on AI products inside the likes of Notion, Vercel, OpenCode, and Amp.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Through a partnership with Baseten, OpenAI also allows the running of cheaper open models. </strong><span>Baseten is one of the leading inference providers, and OpenAI now natively integrates with it. A Baseten statement laid out what this means:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“OpenAI enterprise customers can now use existing OpenAI commitments for open models served by Baseten within Codex or via the Responses API. For enterprises, this means delivering even more intelligence per dollar through your existing OpenAI commitment.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>For now, there’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/364b76e8-f390-474c-b639-89a121835b03?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">an application process</a><span> for becoming a Baseten customer; afterward, you can use open models with zero data retention (ZDR.) Neat!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>OpenAI has made its own subscription a lot more valuable than those of other frontier labs. </strong><span>If you are a customer of Anthropic, you can only allocate spend towards Claude, and on Gemini it’s also only towards Gemini. But OpenAI lets you spend on open models and buy services from their partner network.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This is a clever strategy; they no longer only compete on “who has the best (or cheapest) leading AI model?”, but also on how to spend AI budget efficiently. Clearly, OpenAI will be taking a  cut from spending going towards partners, and those partners will pay – at least initially! – because they’ll expect more business through it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong><span>OpenAI’s approach reminds me a bit of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a38eb5e1-30ac-4305-baf0-59b65d025628?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">AWS marketplace</a><span>: </span></strong><span>AWS also makes it very easy to purchase vendor solutions through its vetted </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a38eb5e1-30ac-4305-baf0-59b65d025628?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">marketplace</a><span>, and sends a single invoice. AWS also surely takes a cut from this: but it’s a winning setup for AWS customers who can integrate services easier with a click, for vendors who get more business, and AWS which provides a more feature-rich platform vs competitors, and generates revenue from taking a cut.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Maybe Anthropic will create its own “partner network”, or keep flying solo by ignoring the rest of the ecosystem. </strong><span>So far, it seems to be against  the idea of allowing Claude Code to integrate with other tools, or for a subsidized Claude subscription (on the $20 or $200 plans) to be used by any harness other than Claude Code. Anthropic also seems hesitant to adopt common standards across AI engineering; for example, it </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4c34d3fd-3d2e-48e5-b1da-cb6aec5eaff4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">took</a><span> 12 months longer than OpenCode, Codex, or Cursor, for Anthropic to add support for the AGENTS.md standard (!!). Until last month, Claude Code only supported the CLAUDE.md file, and it seems like it was Shopify CEO, Tobi Lutke’s, threat to dump Claude Code unless the harness did what every other harness already did, that forced Anthropic to reverse its position:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: But it’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/756ad1b5-216b-4701-a966-90f8961bf155?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">a free model</a><span> for the time being (clearly some promotion, where the anonymous creator pays for usage in some way, as inference is not free), has a 1M context window, and writes good code.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">4. Why CTOs and VPEs are quitting en masse: another take</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>A CTO with 20+ years of experience and who reads Pragmatic Engineer, sent me some notes after reading the article ‘</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/12b84386-9875-440a-99c9-a6a30e81553f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Headed for the exit: the great engineering leader career break</a><span>.’ Asking not to be named, he set out what he sees as an important reason why so many senior engineering leaders are quitting their roles that was missing from the analysis:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“We have all learned how to build great things over time. Also how to find great people to work with. But we’ve also learned how hard it can be to build great things – and we’ve especially found out how hard it is to build great teams.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Fast forward to now. AI is changing how you build great things and how you construct great teams to build things. It’s happening fast. This is great!</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>But this change makes builders want to </strong><em><strong>build</strong></em><strong>. </strong><span>We want to build again...so we can build more, and build faster with better tools, so we can increase the “talent density” of the team by doing more with fewer great people, and so on.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">It’s an amazing time to build things. And it’s only getting better. And people just want to be close to it. They want to build and see how far they can go with these new tools.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>I have a bunch of friends in my social circle who are the “CTO drop outs” you speak of. </strong><span>More still who are moving from management to IC roles in large companies. And their stories are largely what I describe above. They simply see this as a truly exciting time to build.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In the end, building is why they got into this field in the first place.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Basically, lots of CTOs or Head of Engineering folks are using AI to get back to the thing that made them get into computers in the first place. They’re “builders of things” at heart. To build bigger, more complex software, they learned how to build and lead teams; now with AI: what if you can build amazing things with a much smaller team? Lots of these folks would rather do this: start building themselves – then, later – with a much smaller, higher-leveraged team.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>Thanks a lot to the CTO who reached out with this; do leave a comment if their experience resonates with you, on top of other </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/12b84386-9875-440a-99c9-a6a30e81553f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">reasons why folks are leaving</a><span>.</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;hanging-punctuation: allow-end;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin-top: 0;"><em>This post is only for paying subscribers of </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIxODM2NzgzMSwicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3OTA4NzMzMTIsImV4cCI6MjEwNjQ0OTMxMiwiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.FU6cazAZdgmiy6r96ANi8mmsPj3u3ATil2TOZo9YJKM?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin-top: 0;">State is the information a system retains that affects its functionality in some way. For example, a website might keep track of users who have logged in. A document editor remembers the current text. A background worker logs which tasks it has completed and which ones are pending. A database stores the records written to it for as long as needed.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Any useful software usually needs to manage state to carry out its intended functionality. The difficulty is keeping the state correct even as requests overlap, servers are added, machines fail, and software changes are deployed.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Often, the common advice is to “make the application stateless”. But this advice needs explanation. It usually means making particular application servers easy to replace while putting their important state elsewhere. It doesn’t signify a complete absence of state. Understanding such a setup requires looking at why state exists, who owns it, and what happens when it becomes unavailable.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In this article, we will look at why state is the hardest thing in software development and the multiple strategies that developers can use to manage it.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" WorkOS built </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/41c6f135-74da-42b7-b92c-564be05cc17c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Airlock</a><span>, the authorization layer for AI agents. It evaluates every request against the agent’s intent and your rules and either allows it, denies it, or routes it to a human for approval. Works with Claude Code, Codex and MCP gateways. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/41c6f135-74da-42b7-b92c-564be05cc17c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Give it a spin</a><span>.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>In this episode</strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>How is it that a software veteran who regularly shipped ~100K of database-grade code to production each year, pre-AI, feels like he’s even more productive today, with no drop in quality? </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/71ea15ef-aeeb-4039-ac7f-5626fc34deec?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Peter Mattis</a><span> is co-founder and CTO of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/957fe2a7-70a1-45ac-aa6f-f91b317c5061?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Cockroach Labs</a><span>, and an original creator of GIMP. He also worked on Gmail and distributed storage at Google.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In this episode, Peter reflects on his journey from open source to Google to founding a database company, and we explore how to keep systems fast, reliable, and correct at scale, from Gmail’s early storage challenges to the tradeoffs in building distributed databases.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Peter tells us how AI has brought him back to writing code after his work shifted toward management, and why he believes AI can improve quality and multiply the impact of domain experts. We also consider the future of code review, and Peter has some advice about how to level up our engineering skills.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Takeaways from the conversation with Peter</strong></h3><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/02342b0e-c289-4425-adab-b089e75207cc?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/0GzwuYGvKA4" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>1. Peter initially turned down Sergey Brin’s offer to join Google because of the commute. </strong><span>The very first version of the famous Google logo was made in GIMP, the free, open-source raster graphics and image editing software created by Peter and his college roommate Spencer Kimball.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: GIMP</em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In 2001, Sergey reached out to Peter, invited him to an interview and then made an offer. But Peter said “no” because he lived in San Francisco and did not fancy the hour-long commute to Mountain View. Instead, he joined another startup, but that didn’t go anywhere. When Google reached out again, he took the chance.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>2. Peter almost did not ship GIMP after learning about an even more ambitious photo editor. </strong><span>Peter and Spencer worked hard on GIMP, but a few weeks before launching it, they saw an announcement about another program that promised to do everything GIMP did – and then some! Peter and Spencer felt discouraged but shipped anyway – and the rest is history. They never heard about the other ambitious project again. “There’s always going to be someone else working on your idea,” says Peter. “You can’t get dissuaded if they pre-announce it. To founders: assume that dozens of people have the same idea you have, but most won’t ship it! Know that it’s a competition; you’ve got to enjoy that aspect of it – don’t be afraid of it.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>3. B-trees were used in the first version of Gmail. </strong><span>Gmail launched on 1 April 2004, offering 1GB of email storage for free, an offer seen as so ridiculously generous at the time that most people assumed it was an April Fool’s joke! B-trees played a role in Gmail’s storage layer, thanks to storing email threads. Under the hood, each incoming message was matched to a thread using the search index. Threads and their unread counts were tracked by B-trees.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>4. Colossus reduced Google’s file storage overhead by 33%, while increasing redundancy. </strong><span>Before Colossus, Google File System (GFS) stored three full copies of data. For Colossus, which became GFS’s successor, Peter and the team pioneered </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/eb16a47a-2e1e-417f-8baf-c6d832d739eb?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Reed–Solomon erasure coding</a><span> in a distributed file system. Data was stored twice, but redundancy increased!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>5. The fastest way to send a packet around the globe is through space!</strong><span> Peter keeps “speed of light numbers” in his head – similar to what turbopuffer founder Simon Eskildsen does with </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cec4156a-a7a0-4aca-9569-393636a547ba?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">”napkin math” </a><span>calculations. For example, a network round trip within a zone went from milliseconds when Colossus was built to about 100 microseconds today (10x faster!). But sometimes the bottleneck is the speed of light, and as light speed is faster in a vacuum than anywhere else, that means the fastest global route is straight up to Starlink, across by laser, and then back down. Find out more in ‘</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a7837eb1-5876-40cc-b4aa-e0d15267fd8e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Delay is not an option: low latency routing in space</a><span>’.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>6. Peter twice “beat” standard library data structures in performance terms.</strong><span> At Google, one of his colleagues noticed that std::map showed up in memory profiles. Peter looked closer and figured out that the std::map implementation is a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/72f16184-6992-49eb-b962-6d6f6ae0e2b9?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">red-black tree</a><span>, meaning every node has two pointers. Peter built a B-tree with nearly the same semantics which was both faster, due to spatial locality, and smaller because it used fewer pointers. They used this data structure inside Google. Peter also did something similar with Go’s map: it was performant, but he built a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bdf73a48-de89-403a-aca3-ffee6b3b3748?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Swiss Table</a><span> implementation that was faster. That implementation later made it into the Go library, with the Go team helping to finish it!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>7. If you squint hard, everything in distributed databases and storage systems starts looking like a B-tree. </strong><span>These B-trees are a recurring theme in this podcast episode: the backend of Gmail, the std::map replacement, CockroachDB’s range index, etc. There’s even a paper on this phenomenon, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/456e5ca9-0184-4667-b223-c9b5089d4745?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Ubiquitous B-Tree</a><span>.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table With primary and secondary replicas, neither one will know if the other received the last write following a crash. So, CockroachDB uses three replicas by default – and up to five for some system tables – and customers can add more, although this will result in higher latency.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>9. CockroachDB’s design was inspired by Google’s Colossus data storage system and Spanner. </strong><span>Colossus was append-only, meaning you could only add to files and not mutate them. Google’s distributed database, Spanner, was built on top of Colossus, and so Spanner’s design decisions came from Colossus’ append-only nature. But if you cannot update files and only append to them, it’s not possible to use B-trees as the database’s design structure since B-trees need the files to be updated. An ideal data structure for append-only filesystems is the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1ac17384-4095-49aa-b0dd-875150d33d3f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: RocksDB was the underlying storage engine that CockroachDB used in its early years. In 2019, Peter wrote and open sourced </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3f51ed9f-dd15-412f-a9c9-e26200a8c8a5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Pebble</a><span>, which is now CockroachDB’s storage engine.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>10. Peter, the former C++ readability reviewer at Google, predicts we will stop reviewing code: </strong><span>At Google, every code change needs to be signed off for “readability” by a language readability reviewer, and Peter was a C++ readability reviewer for years. But these days, he’s reviewing less code and foresees this continuing. As he puts it: “What I’m finding is the agents are getting better; you’re having to give less and less scrutiny. I don’t know if it’s going to be this year or next, [but] we’re materially going to stop looking at the code in the same way we don’t look at assembly anymore.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>11. Non-engineers at Cockroach Labs built ~1,000 internal apps (!!) in a couple of months.</strong><span> Earlier this year, Cockroach Labs launched an internal platform for non-devs to build apps (think of it as an “internal Lovable”). Folks jumped at it; HR professionals built new tools they’d only dreamt of, while the CFO created the dashboards they’d always longed for, and many others too. Peter and the engineering team were surprised at this uptake, but it chimes with how OpenAI saw nearly all its non-engineers move almost their entire token spend from ChatGPT to Codex within just 4 months.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>12. Does “flow” still exist with AI? </strong><span>I asked Peter this, and he believes it does, but it’s different from the “coding flow” state: “It definitely feels a bit different. It’s maybe a bit less intense, but you’re managing more things cognitively. I’m thinking of ideas that normally would’ve taken me a week to experiment with. And I think of multiple of these experiments and then fire them off all simultaneously. [It feels as] if I was a college professor with a whole swarm of research assistants, and they’re all off doing things and it’s coming back </span><em>really</em><span> rapidly.”</span></p><h3 This involves the use of tools. While MCP made it easier to expose these tools, there were a lot of other concerns that had to be handled in order to make it work at an enterprise level.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">DoorDash built a shared Agent Gateway to control how AI agents discover and use tools. The gateway brings together several responsibilities: checking permissions, managing credentials, choosing which tools an agent can see, forwarding requests, and recording what happened.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In this article, we will look at how the DoorDash engineering team built this gateway and the decisions they made. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why an AI Agent Needs Tools</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A language model can write a super-detailed explanation of how to investigate a software problem, but it doesn’t automatically have access to a company’s code repositories, incident reports, or production logs. We need to provide access to those systems through software. From the perspective of the model, these systems are like tools.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">An AI agent is an application that uses a language model to decide which steps and tools to use while working on a particular task. A tool is a specific capability that the application makes available to the model. For example, searching documentation, reading a support ticket, and opening a pull request.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">When the model selects a tool, the surrounding application uses the tool to execute the required operation and supplies the result back to the language model. The model can then use that result to decide what to do next. For example, an agent investigating a failed software build might retrieve the build logs, inspect relevant code, and use what it finds to explain the failure.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Some tools only read information. Others can also change something in a real system, such as updating a ticket or creating a pull request. This makes tool access a very important part of an agent’s design. It determines what the agent can learn and what it can eventually do with that learning. At DoorDash, these capabilities come from many places, including internal services, engineering systems, documentation platforms, and third-party software.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why MCP Is Not Enough</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Different systems or tools normally expose different interfaces. An API is a way for one program to request information or actions from another program. Without a shared approach, an AI agent application has to accommodate the particular interfaces of every tool it uses.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The Model Context Protocol (MCP) provides a common way to describe, discover, and invoke capabilities. An MCP server exposes tools, and an MCP client communicates with that server. The agent application uses an MCP client to access the tools.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width:
