rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">With the decision to go all-in on native with AI, the e-commerce business is committing to migrate all of its apps. With AI, it should be faster than the migration to React Native was. Mustafa, again:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“We are going to migrate all our mobile apps to Swift and Kotlin using AI throughout the process.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Shop has already shipped as a fully native app in just 12 weeks, the Shopify app is underway, and the rest will follow soon</strong><span>. We’re moving quickly, but not by lowering the bar.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Every rebuild must meet or exceed the performance, stability, accessibility, and product quality people expect today. This isn’t just the same apps rewritten in different languages. We’re rebuilding them so both humans and agents can understand, test, and change them quickly.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Best of luck to the team with this migration! I’m looking forward to hearing about what they learn with this move.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">4. Haven’t we seen this back-and-forth before?</h2><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>It’s big news in dev circles that Shopify has decided to go all-in on native, but I have a sense of déjà vu in terms of an enthusiastic onboarding to React Native, later followed by churning. It happened with Airbnb. A decade ago in 2016, it moved on to React Native. Their engineering team </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/08d9f761-9f74-4642-99d7-438fb06d5743?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">reflected</a><span> on the move:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“In 2016, one of [the technologies we took a bet on] was React Native. Back then, we recognized how important mobile was becoming to our business but simply didn’t have enough mobile engineers to reach our goals. As a result, we began to explore alternative options. Our website is built primarily with React. It has been a highly effective and universally liked web framework within Airbnb. Because of this, we saw React Native as an opportunity to open up mobile development to more engineers as well as ship code more quickly by leveraging its cross-platform nature.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Between 2016 and 2018, Airbnb was all-in on React Native and lots of things worked well:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Shared code: </strong><span>the company achieved ~95% shared code between the platforms</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Unified design language system:</strong><span> a shared design system, between the two platforms.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Iteration speed</strong><span>: hot reload made it faster to develop and debug</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Performance</strong><span>: Airbnb was happy with React Native’s performance</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Animations</strong><span>: a frequent worry. However, these were jank-free for Airbnb</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Then RN is dropped for native</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Despite these working well, there were also several issues:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>Maintaining an RN fork</strong><span>: Airbnb found the RN ecosystem immature at the time, and had to frequently fork the library, make their changes, then contribute it back upstream. Painful!</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>JavaScriptCore problems</strong><span>: back then, React Native ran on top of the JavaScript core engine, which had consistency problems, which the Hermes runtime has since mostly fixed.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><strong>App size</strong><span>: React Native adds to the binary size – and going native shrinks it. Shopify also felt the benefit of native in terms of binary size.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Amusingly, RN made hiring harder. </strong><span>Airbnb found it difficult to hire iOS and Android engineers due to being associated with React Native. As Gabriel Peal, a senior software engineer there at the time, wrote:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“Through word of mouth in the community, many people began to associate Airbnb with React Native and some even believed that our app was 100% React Native. Even though this was far from the truth, many Android and iOS engineers were hesitant to apply to Airbnb as a result.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Obviously, this was when React Native was more niche and native iOS/Android more mainstream, and it was simple to hire iOS or Android engineers by paying near the top of market.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Lower app quality than their own bar allows is what probably pushed Airbnb to abandon RN. </strong><span>Airbnb’s engineering team </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fe18446a-d2e1-4217-bad4-e7d02099bd22?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">gave a few reasons</a><span> – like not moving much faster than when developing native, or still needing a similar-sized engineering team as before – but overall, my sense is that the React Native of 2018 didn’t live up to design and quality standards at the short-term rental giant, so they moved back to native.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>It seems like times change but other things don’t, as Shopify is quitting for the same reason Airbnb did eight years ago: the performance of the framework caused by unavoidable overhead. React Native’s performance is a </span><em>lot</em><span> better these days, but AI changes things. It has brought down the overhead of building native iOS/Android apps and made it a </span><em>lot</em><span> smaller. React Native loses out by comparison, nulling its performance gains.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">5. Going native since 2019</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Shortly after Shopify announced its decision to quit RN, Notion posted that they are also moving to native and showed some improvements from their non-native implementation:</p><div class="video-player-with-background is-static video-player-wrapper" role="region" aria-label="Video player" style="flex-grow: 1;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin-top: 0.5em;"><a class="video-player video-player-with-background" href="https://substack.com/redirect/e7b2773d-e7f0-45c8-aad2-54586d327abb?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;display: block;width: 100%;cursor: pointer;background-color: rgb(0,0,0);height: auto;border-radius: 8px;padding-bottom: 0"><img class="video-player-preview" width="550" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!MzPl!,w_1100,h_618,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/l_play_button_usfui2,w_144,e_colorize:0/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-video.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fvideo_upload%2Fpost%2F218028942%2F536092bd-2689-4749-9c83-9781e0a21080%2Ftranscoded-00001.png" alt="" data-component-name="VideoPlayer-PreviewImg" data-testid="video-player-static-preview-image" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;top: 0;left: 0;width: 100%;max-height: 100%;background: black;cursor: pointer;object-fit: contain;position: relative;border-radius: 8px;"></a></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><em>Notion loading times: before (with React) and after (fully native). Fully native is visibly snappier.</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Plenty of posts on this topic assumed that Notion was talking about moving from React Native to native, but that wasn’t the case, as covered in a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2db6b3d9-e30e-4944-a8e9-3c8b3e23fd0b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">podcast episode with Notion’s mobile team</a><span>. Instead, Notion has taken a more twisty route:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Until 2019, Notion’s app used Cordova, which is a wrapper around mobile web</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">From 2019, two engineers started to migrate Cordova pages one at a time to native</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Progress was incremental and slow to avoid breaking the app</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">By 2024, most pages had been migrated by a team of 11 native engineers among 600 engineers at  Notion</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Most complex was the editor page in React, and the mobile app wrapped around it. This was left until last</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Notion’s native rewrite of the editor is continuing today, and AI tools haven’t “magically” sped up the process. </strong><span>The editor screen is by far the most complex and feature-rich, and Notion has not completed the project yet, but they’re getting closer. As the mobile team rewrites the editor, the web team keeps adding new features, which the mobile team then needs to support. Also, the editor will have a bunch of hidden complexity, such as:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">“Older” Notion document markups need to be supported, so the native editor must also support retired markup.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Some things are especially tricky to build for touch interfaces, like managing tables</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Notion’s native team surely had to write their own UI rendering library from scratch: the built-in UIKit or ComposeKit will not have been feature rich for their use cases</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;"><span>… it’s extremely complex to build a native editor on mobile: I know because my brother built Craft Docs. Its editor was native from the start which made it hard to build, initially! Check out the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b29bfaff-a68c-4849-ab01-646f0cc39860?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">podcast</a><span>.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Notion’s delay in going native has spared everyone a ton of backwards compatibility headaches. </strong><span>Once Notion’s iOS and Android app would go fully native, Notion could no longer roll out editor updates on the fly as now. Below are the differences between the current, webview wrapped, React, and native Notion support for a new, imaginary UI primitive called “tables with AI filtering”:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Webview-wrapped React: Notion rolls it out to the web; it’s live for all mobile users! Hooray, zero confusion, and near-zero work (beyond testing that the mobile app works as expected)</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Native mobile: Notion has to build the feature ahead of time for native</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">→ ship it 2-4 weeks before to the App Store</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">→ hide it behind a feature flag</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">→ enable the feature flag when the web version is live</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">→ deal with customer complaints about not seeing the new feature for those who have not updated the app</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">→ worry about the experience of customers who might never update the app</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">→ … slow down web product development to allow for mobile to go at the same speed, which is slower by design due to App Store review requirements.</p></li></ul></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">6. Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) would like a word</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Shopify chose to drop React Native in order to get more control over performance and over the platform-level with native, and to skip multiple abstraction layers that React Native adds into the application.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>There’s also another way to keep UI code native Swift or Kotlin while sharing business logic: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f58d7a9d-bb2d-42d9-b80d-1f3acbaed1ea?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Kotlin Multiplatform</a><span>. It allows the writing of business logic for both iOS and Android apps: once in Kotlin, and then the code is called from Swift in the iOS app.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1416" style="text-align: 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em><span>Kotlin Multiplatform at a high level. Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b2dcbad8-5c66-4f73-bffa-576a4d7e9e82?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;">Building Mobile Apps at Scale</a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Kotlin Multiplatform was released in 2017 by JetBrains and declared stable and production-ready in 2023. It supports not only iOS and Android, but also using the same business logic in web apps; a nice bonus addition.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>But KMP does take time to onboard to. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1699ab42-7f71-458b-b7ad-f17b217b51bf?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Here’s Duolingo Staff</a><span> engineer John Rodriguez on how they started to move over:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“The initial, native implementation of Adventures [a feature inside Duolingo] took five months on Android. We spent those months really figuring out how to put this into KMP and building that iOS layer on top of it. And then finally, with the KMP library built out, it was just 1.5 more months to get the web port working. And to clarify, these are engineering months – so a sum of all engineering time.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Then, for another feature, they also decided to port to KMP. John again:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“The iOS native implementation for Video Call took nine months. We managed to get WebSockets on KMP within 1 month. And then the full Android port took six engineering months after that.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">So, KMP is still a bunch of work to get right, even with the benefit of much more Kotlin code-sharing between iOS and Android, and full control of native rendering and UI layouts.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>One very good use case for KMP is when the business logic error could be catastrophic. </strong><span>In this case, writing the business logic once in Kotlin, validating it with various tests, and then making sure both iOS, Android – and perhaps even web! – uses the same code. Also, when a team has AI “rewrite” the core business logic for different platforms, there’s always a chance that the business logic is rewritten with a small bug which causes issues. Plus, it’s harder to debug when the business logic can be slightly different on iOS, Android, and the web.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>KMP does have its own downsides, needless to say. </strong><span>Shopify evaluated KMP before settling on native. Mustafa Ali told me:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">“KMP has its own limitations. On iOS, every separately packaged KMP module has its own garbage collector. When multiple collectors run at the same time, they cause severe slowdowns and deadlocks making the app unusable. The solution to this is creating an umbrella framework to package all modules into a single one, but that brings its own packaging and build tradeoffs.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Debugging also gets more cumbersome when a failure crosses Kotlin, Swift, generated interop, and multiple toolchains. Kotlin-level debugging in Xcode relies on third-party tooling, and the LLDB integration was extremely slow in our testing. Agents can help investigate these issues, but they still have to reason through the same runtime and tooling boundaries.”</p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">7. What’s next?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Shopify dumping RN is a big story because Shopify has been the most vocal and prominent supporter of React Native, and a massive contributor to the project! Now, they are out.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Nearly four years ago, I </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/38987cd4-222b-47ca-ab24-229afc50489a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">covered</a><span> a fall in native mobile recruitment by startups, as more small companies chose the likes of React Native and Flutter for mobile application development. In our cross-platform deepdive last year, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/232d0eea-c8e4-4153-b8f3-cda977212022?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">we found</a><span> that US startups are more likely to use React Native than to use Flutter, and the impression was that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4b3e5e36-34c0-471a-b2e7-bea93e507565?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Expo was the platform</a><span> of choice for mid-sized-and-above companies due to developer tooling missing from React Native.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">But with AI getting so good at native mobile generation, I suspect the whole trend of needing to hire iOS, Android, or React Native engineers will change to a focus on recruiting “generalist” engineers. I wonder if the importance of native vs cross-platform will start to fade as AI continues to be adopted.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Let’s review the options for building cross-platform apps:</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>React Native: still a solid option, also with AI. </strong><span>Meta continues to invest heavily in the technology and use some of it inside its apps – although the key parts of Facebook, Messenger and Instagram are all native – while Coinbase remains a widely-cited </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9aa8038b-2610-43cb-a449-214ae255018e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">React Native success story</a><span>, along with </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/66bf081c-761e-43d8-99f0-f89bbe1ea9e1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Discord and its RN move.</a></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Native: much more viable than before, but it’s very early for AI + native. </strong><span>Shopify has a history of bold engineering moves and going all-in without worrying too much about the additional work of onboarding to a new tech stack or approach. They did this with Ruby on Rails, React Native, and now with AI + native mobile development.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>I have no doubt that things will work out fine for Shopify,</span><em> </em><span>but that doesn’t mean this approach is necessarily the right one for other teams without similar energy and willingness to figure things out themselves.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Kotlin Multiplatform: feels surprisingly relevant, especially with AI! </strong><span>The downside of going native is that it’s hard to verify that the iOS and Android business logic works in the same way and that the two apps operate identically. Shopify needed to build a test suite to test both apps, and to keep running AI checks to spot when the codebases diverge in functionality.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In contrast, Kotlin Multiplatform ensures that the business logic is the same because both iOS and Android use the same code! And it does this at no real hit to native performance, as the UI is still fully native code.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">There’s been hesitation from iOS devs to onboard to KMP because Kotlin is the language that Android devs are most familiar with. But when AI can write Kotlin as well as it can Swift, is this a big deal any more?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Flutter: an alternative, but what does it offer that React Native and native don’t? </strong><span>Flutter is Google’s version of React Native. The biggest downside is that you need to learn – well, your agent needs to use – a completely new programming language called Dart that’s different from React, Swift, and Kotlin. That means adding yet another abstraction layer – which used to be a problem for software engineers to learn.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">But with agents writing most of the code, I’m sure using Dart would be less of an issue. Then again, if you’re using agents to build apps, why use an abstraction at all instead of going directly to native?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>The elephant in the room is Apple’s incredibly strict review process, unchanged since 2008. </strong><span>The reason the whole mobile industry is stuck on weekly releases (at the most frequent!) is because Apple explicitly bans any meaningful updates from going around their App Store review process. Due to this strict process, even though it’s theoretically possible to ship live updates to React Native apps, doing so would risk Apple banning applications for bypassing its App Store review process.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Takeaways</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>Mobile engineering is being changed by AI agents able to generate pretty good code in major programming languages, and now also for native iOS and Android. The decision by Shopify to move its e-commerce business away from RN is a sign of how AI agents are changing the equation for teams by now being </span><em>very</em><span> capable at mobile coding.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>Until now, recruitment and costs were major concerns for mobile development.</strong><span> Tech companies that could pay top-of-market and attract senior+ mobile engineers, and were willing to spend on mobile development, did hire individual iOS, Android, and web engineers. The likes of Uber, Airbnb, and Square, took on the task of coordinating three separate “frontend” teams, and delivered the highest-quality, most performant mobile apps.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">But that wasn’t the case for most places.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The arrival of AI means any software engineer can potentially write good enough iOS or Android code – and do both in parallel. Specialist hiring may no longer be a limiting factor, which is what Shopify is betting on.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>It’s worth asking about the downside of going native on iOS </strong><em><strong>and</strong></em><strong> Android. </strong><span>In the best case, you’ll have a process where the iOS and Android codebase remain in-sync with some help from AI, there’s a single test harness for both apps, and you retain full control over the performance and architecture of apps on both platforms.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In the worst case, you learn a lot about the limitations of AI and mobile, and might have a codebase that is problematic on iOS, Android, or both. But there’s an incentive to get better at native iOS + Android development, using agents. And you remain in full control of the code with no dependence on additional abstractions. This approach forces better mobile engineering, regardless!</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><strong>“Works on one platform, works on all platforms” is still a strong case for non-native approaches, though. </strong><span>Going native with the help of AI agents means you </span><em>need</em><span> to build a testing environment to ensure that both iOS and Android work as expected and exactly like each other.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>But what if you don’t want to build and maintain a separate testing environment? In this case, sticking with React Native or Flutter is probably a better approach! Plus, there is the argument to be made that React Native and Flutter are mature enough when it comes to performance, and minimizing overhead. Plus, agents could build a RN or Flutter app and have it work on both platforms consistently, like just human devs. Also, it’s a valid point that if </span><em>consistency</em><span> is more important than </span><em>platform native look and feel, </em><span>then you are still probably better off using React Native or Flutter. To be honest, simple apps don’t need to feel all that native!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Do you build mobile apps? Let us know what approaches you’re considering, and whether AI tools are being used to experiment with new ways to build apps. Leave a comment below.</p><p class="button-wrapper" Without traces, you are guessing.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><span>In this hands-on workshop, Serge from Sentry instruments three agents with Sentry Agent Tracing: a chatbot in an ecommerce store, a custom Slack agent, and a GitHub Action that reviews PRs. Let’s assume that the assistant responds immediately by explaining that the company offers a 30-day refund window, describes the cancellation process, and promises that the money will arrive within five working days. All of it sounds quite helpful, confident, and complete.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">But there is just one problem.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In reality, the company only allows refunds within 14 days. Also, there is no promise about the 5-day processing time. The assistant has actually taken bits of a plausible policy and invented a fake commitment out of thin air. In other words, it has lied. The customer now expects something that the company never offered.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Though this example might sound fictitious, it shows one of the most important problems in applications built with LLMs. While LLMs can produce excellent language, they can get the underlying information totally wrong.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In this article, we will look at why this problem of hallucinations happens with LLMs and the techniques that can help make LLMs more dependable for answering. Actually Means</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Hallucination in the context of LLMs is generated information that is factually incorrect, invented, or inconsistent with the material the model is supposed to use. Here’s how a hallucination is happens:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table plaintext;">The entire response may not be wrong. In fact, an otherwise useful explanation can contain a single fabricated date, an unsupported promise, or a reference to a document that doesn’t exist. That small detail may be the part the reader relies upon.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">We can’t outright call this behavior lying, but it comes pretty close to a lie. The answer resembles a confident falsehood. However, lying usually implies an intention to deceive. A hallucination doesn’t establish that intention. The model can produce an incorrect answer through its normal generation process. In the support example from earlier, the immediate problem is that the application presents an incorrect generated policy as established company information.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The context matters a lot here. Inventing a refund policy for a fictional company is appropriate when the task asks for one. However, presenting that same invention as the policy of an actual business is a factual failure. Ultimately, the difference is more about what the answer claims to represent.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Three Ways an Answer Can Go Wrong</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The AI support assistant’s errors become easier to reason about when divided into three useful categories:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">A factual hallucination contradicts reality. For example, saying that the company’s refund window is 30 days, when it is actually 14, belongs here. The company exists and has a real policy, but the assistant describes it incorrectly.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">A faithfulness hallucination concerns the relationship between the answer and its supplied evidence. For example, if the application provides a policy requiring an unused account, but the assistant says usage does not matter, it has contradicted its source.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;unicode-bidi: plaintext;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin: 0;">Fabrication involves inventing something such as a policy section, a confirmation number, or a research paper.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">These three categories overlap.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">How Predicting Text Produces Hallucinations</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">To understand the mechanism clearly, let us look at how an LLM builds a particular response.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">As you may be aware, LLMs process text in small units called tokens. A token can be a word, part of a word, or punctuation. For a given input and the response generated so far, the model calculates probabilities for the possible next tokens. A generation method selects one, adds it to the response, and repeats the whole process once again. Depending on the settings, selection may choose the most likely token or sample among possible continuations.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A likely continuation is not the same thing as a verified statement. The probability used to select the next token concerns text generation. It doesn’t certify the entire answer. Likewise, words such as “certainly” and “definitely” are generated language. Their presence cannot establish that the model has checked the policy or possesses reliable evidence.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The model learns these patterns during training.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">In the initial stage, called pretraining, it works through large amounts of text and learns to predict continuations. Its internal numerical settings, known as parameters or weights, gradually capture patterns involving grammar, concepts, relationships, and facts. This produces useful knowledge and the ability to handle many different language tasks.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">However, familiarity with a subject cannot establish every specific fact about it. A model may encounter 1000s of refund policies mentioning 14 days, 30 days, unused accounts, and processing delays. Those examples help it discuss refunds in an appropriate way. But they don’t tell anything about which conditions apply to this particular customer at this particular company.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Something similar happens with fabricated citations. The model learns what a research reference looks like, including author names, publication years, and technical titles. It can reproduce that structure without having a real reference to back things up.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why Models Struggle to Admit Uncertainty</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">LLMs are mainly optimized for plausible text. They receive additional training to improve accuracy, helpfulness, and responses to uncertainty. Still, a fluent continuation doesn’t prove that every statement made by the LLM is true.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Some training incentives can also encourage guessing. For example, consider an evaluation approach that awards a point for a correct answer but gives the same score to a wrong answer and an admission of uncertainty. In this way, guessing offers some chance of receiving a point. Abstaining from guessing means zero points. This incentive trains the model to guess, resulting in hallucinations.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">However, it isn’t totally correct to say that hallucinations are unavoidable because they are built into the architecture. Models can recognize some uncertainty and detect some mistakes. Models have useful self-evaluation abilities under particular conditions, together with limitations when those abilities must generalize to unfamiliar tasks. However, there is no dependable internal guarantee that separates every correct answer from every guess.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Asking the model for a confidence percentage also cannot automatically solve this problem. For example, a response claiming 95% confidence needs evidence that such scores are meaningful for the task. Calibration measures whether confidence estimates match observed accuracy across many cases. Without that evaluation, an impressive percentage can add another vague detail to an already uncertain answer.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Giving the Model Evidence with RAG</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The first major defense addresses missing information directly.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) finds relevant material and adds it to the model’s input before generation. Retrieval finds the information, augmentation supplies it, and generation produces the answer.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px plaintext;">In our example support application, a refund question triggers a search through approved company documents. The application retrieves passages describing the applicable policy and adds them alongside the question. The assistant now has the company’s actual conditions available while writing its response.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">This changes what a useful and valid answer looks like. For example, the retrieved policy makes it clear that the purchase must fall within 14 days and that the account must be unused for the refund to be valid. The customer’s query establishes only the purchase timing. The assistant should recognize that one condition remains unresolved.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">RAG still has failure points. A search can return a retired policy, choose the wrong product’s policy, or miss an exception. The model can also misread a correct passage or add an unsupported promise.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For this application, documents need clear product names, effective dates, and approval status. Conflicting policies need explicit handling so that the model can know which one is applicable.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Document preparation also includes keeping related conditions together. Suppose the refund period appears at the end of one passage while the unused-account requirement begins the next. Retrieving only the first passage can leave the assistant with an incomplete rule. Regularly checking what the model actually receives helps distinguish a retrieval problem from a failure to interpret complete evidence.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Looking Up the Missing Facts with Tools</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Documents explain general rules, but the LLM-based assistant also needs facts about the individual customer. This is where tool use becomes very important.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A tool lets the application obtain information or perform a defined operation outside the model’s scope. Examples include searching the web, retrieving an account record, and running a calculation. Interaction with external information sources can reduce errors on evaluated tasks.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">An API provides a defined way for one program to request information or actions from another. The support application might offer an account-lookup API that returns the purchase date and whether the subscription has been used. The model requests the lookup, the application executes it, and the returned result becomes available for generating a proper answer.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">RAG and tool use can overlap because document retrieval can itself be exposed as a tool. In this example, they supply complementary evidence. The policy states the conditions, while the account lookup supplies the customer facts needed to apply them.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The important thing is that the lookup must actually happen. A generated sentence saying that the account was checked doesn’t prove anything. If the tool fails, that failure must remain visible to the application. Assuming that the account is unused would simply introduce a hallucination at a different point.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Eligibility and payment are separate facts as well. Even after confirming that a customer qualifies, the assistant cannot truthfully say that a refund has been issued until the payment system reports success. Generating a made-up confirmation number doesn’t create a transaction. The application needs the actual operation and its outcome before describing that action as completed.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Writing Useful Answers</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Another defense to hallucinations is to make insufficient evidence a valid outcome.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Explicit instructions can tell the assistant to identify missing information and avoid unsupported conclusions. We can disallow uncertainty by restricting answers to supplied material when appropriate, and grounding claims in supporting passages. These measures can reduce hallucinations, but they don’t eliminate them.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Either way, doing so is more helpful than a bare admission of ignorance. In our example, the assistant can explain that the purchase falls within the 14-day window while account usage still needs checking. This preserves the information already established and identifies the exact obstacle to a complete answer.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" href="https://substack.com/redirect/ef628b01-916e-403e-84aa-117d2baeeb7d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The software also needs a way to represent that outcome. Requiring every response to contain either “eligible” or “ineligible” leaves no room for missing evidence. A third state, such as “needs review,” allows uncertainty to influence the application’s next action.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Why an Explanation Is Not Proof</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Another proposed defense is chain-of-thought prompting, which asks a model to work through a problem in intermediate steps.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Breaking a task into smaller parts can improve some answers and make mistakes easier to notice. However, a generated explanation may contain false premises or fail to faithfully describe what influenced the result.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For example, suppose the assistant explains that the customer purchased 15 days ago, the refund window is 30 days, and the customer therefore qualifies. The argument is easy to follow, but it depends on the wrong policy. More explanation doesn’t supply the missing fact.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">A useful application instead requests a concise justification connected to checkable evidence. The assistant identifies the policy clause, the relevant account information, and how the conditions apply. This gives a reviewer concrete claims to inspect without treating the explanation itself as proof.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Checking the Answer Before It Reaches the Customer</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Verification makes inspection a separate part of the workflow. This is because drafting an answer, generating verification questions, and answering those questions independently reduced hallucinations on the evaluated tasks. This supports structured checking, while leaving open the possibility that the checker also makes mistakes.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For the support assistant example, the sentence “The customer qualifies for a refund that will arrive within five days” contains separate claims. Eligibility requires the policy and account facts. Processing time needs its own supporting evidence. If nothing establishes the five-day promise, that promise should be removed.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Citations make these checks easier, provided the citations are checked too. A document must exist, apply to the question, and support the particular statement attached to it. The application can construct links from retrieved document identifiers and check whether quoted passages occur in those documents. Just placing a real link beside an unsupported claim remains an unreliable answer.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Some simpler techniques are also present, but they have narrower benefits.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Lowering temperature generally concentrates token sampling more strongly on likely continuations, but it doesn’t establish factual accuracy. The assistant may become more consistent while repeating the same wrong policy. Requiring a particular output format also helps software process a response without proving that its contents are correct.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">For unambiguous rules, ordinary application code can perform part of the decision. If the policy has clearly defined conditions, code can compare the verified purchase date and usage status against those conditions. The model can then explain the result. However, exceptions and ambiguous policy language still require explicit handling.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Conclusion</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The improved support workflow with fewer hallucinations can be thought of as having a clear sequence.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">It retrieves the applicable policy, obtains the necessary account facts, checks the conditions, and prepares an explanation. It then checks the explanation’s factual claims and citations. If some information is missing, it generates a specific unresolved status. Lastly, cases requiring judgment are routed for further review.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">The reliability of such a setup must be measured on realistic examples. Test cases should include eligible purchases, used accounts, missing records, outdated policies, and questions containing false assumptions. A customer asking how to claim a “guaranteed 30-day refund” should not cause the assistant to accept that guarantee without checking.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;">Evaluation also needs to consider usefulness. An assistant that always answers may make unsupported claims, while one that always declines provides little value. We should measure whether delivered answers are correct and supported, whether unanswerable cases are handled appropriately, and whether answerable questions are declined unnecessarily.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;unicode-bidi: plaintext;margin-bottom: 0;">Returning to the original customer, the LLM-based assistant can now explain which conditions are satisfied, which remain unresolved, and what evidence supports its response. The wording may be less confident when information is missing, but the answer becomes more useful. A developer’s responsibility is to build a process in which the evidence determines what the application can claim in a responsible manner.</p></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Healthy Feedback

Anuja Karnik

“Peer-to-peer feedback is a powerful growth tool, and yet candid feedback is rare. We treat all feedback as positive - either to strengthen confidence or improve effectiveness. Based on this principle we can form several patterns for both giving and receiving feedback to help teams improve their interactions.”

#Management TeamHealth Feedback
item.description: Healthy Feedback

item.title: Ten Things Nobody Tells You When You Become A Manager
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Ten Things Nobody Tells You When You Become A Manager

Louise Deason

(1) Your job has changed. (2) Stop doing the work. (3) Learn for a month. (4) Accept that you are now the weather. (5) Let them run the 1:1. (6) Embrace the shit. (7) Work out what your new manager wants. (8) Give the hard feedback early. (9) Keep receipts for your people. (10) Know what seat you've taken.

#Management NewManager Tips
item.description: Ten Things Nobody Tells You When You Become A Manager

item.ns0:encoded:
Managing Systems

Sunil Sadasivan

“This seems complex, but it’s actually quite simple, and I believe it’s the key to being a successful strategic thinker in systems and organizations. This model works in every system I can think of — applications and products, computing systems of limited resources, and people, teams and large-scale organizations.”

#Leadership OrgDesign Strategy

item.title: You Should All Be Asking Way More Questions

Sean Goedecke

“When someone is explaining something to me, I ask on average one question every thirty seconds. I’m sure this is frustrating to some people, but it’s actually a good habit and you should do it too.”

#CareerGrowth Communication

optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;">What is MPP?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If we take the human out of the payment flow, something has to fill the gap. MPP, or Machine Payments Protocol, is the thing that fills this gap.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">MPP was co-authored by Stripe and Tempo, and launched on 18th March, 2026. The core of the MPP specification has been published as the Payment HTTP Authentication Schema and has been submitted to the IETF standards track. This is the same body that also maintains HTTP.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">What exactly does MPP do?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Before any money moves between two parties, they need to agree to a few things. For example, what is the cost of a service, what counts as payment, and what the proof of payment should look like.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">As we discussed, humans make all these decisions just by looking. A user opens a page, finds the price, recognizes the checkout button, and knows what to do next.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Now, MPP manages each of these decisions. It also gives a specific name to each of them:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The Challenge is what the server asks for (payment) when someone requests a service.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The Credential is what the client sends back as proof.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The Receipt is what the server returns along with the service delivery.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">These three objects (Challenge, Credential, and Receipt) form the core of the protocol along with payment intents around charge, session, and subscription.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" the internet has a slightly different way of presenting the payment details to the users. In the case of humans, it rarely matters, because people are good at figuring things out. Software cannot do that. It needs the terms in the same place and format every time so that it can parse the details efficiently.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Therefore, MPP places these details in HTTP headers.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The server sends its terms back in a WWW-Authenticate: Payment header. The client returns the proof in an Authorization: Payment header. The server finally confirms with a Payment-Receipt header. The Challenge contains details such as an ID, the amount, the currency, who to pay, which payment method, and the validity of the offer.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" governed separately. Each rail (card networks, blockchain, payment processor) can write and maintain its own specification for how it fits the core. This makes the protocol open enough so that it isn’t controlled by individual companies. The protocol itself is free, with no licensing fees for implementing it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The ultimate goal of MPP is to become the language of internet payments. A service that understands MPP can sell to any agent. An agent that understands MPP can buy from any service. Neither one has to have heard of the other beforehand.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;">How Does MPP Work?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">When an agent requests your API or service, your service returns an HTTP 402 response with payment details. The agent authorizes the payment, retries the request, and gets access to the paid resource along with a receipt. The diagram below shows the overall process flow:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/6d19cd7a-7848-4cdf-b9e9-9930ec9170d1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction:
