Emoji', 'Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: 400;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em><span>Before we start, a special announcement to paid subscribers: if you’re in San Francisco on Thursday, 5 November, join me on the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/38ce79e0-285d-4fa1-baf7-576ca504ca96?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">System Update with The Pragmatic Engineer event</a><span>. This is an evening with OpenAI, Linear and DoorDash and myself, organized by Sentry. We get into what AI-augmented automations they’re running in prod, and how it’s going, in an off-the record and raw conversation. Seats are limited, but as a paid subscriber, I’m aiming to prioritize your RSVP: please you use the code TODO</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>AI is changing how us software engineers build software, and developers’ tool preferences are rapidly evolving with it – like how AI coding harnesses have gotten very popular. Likewise, future versions of the world’s leading operating systems look certain to feature more support for agentic tools.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To find out how things are changing, we talked with the folks at tech giant Microsoft who shared in detail their plan for Windows, and how AI will play a part. It comes after the company’s previous AI efforts led to it being dubbed “Microslop” by some users online.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Windows team’s vision is opinionated and includes building new agentic primitives, alongside reversing some decisions that have annoyed engineers. Microsoft wants developers who have shunned the system to return. The big question is: will it succeed?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For more, check out a previous article on how </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fa762701-df41-4c7f-bb51-025eae16539a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>the leading Linux distribution, Ubuntu, is changing, thanks to AI</span></a><span>, with a focus on hardware support for GPUs, NPUs and DPUs, a bet on local-first LLMs, and a focus on AI developer tools.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today, we cover:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>How many devs use Windows anyway? </span></strong><span>It’s hard to get exact numbers, but macOS appears far more popular at startups than Windows, while Linux may also be on track to overtake Microsoft’s OS in developer popularity.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Agent identity & discovery.</span></strong><span> Windows ships with native support for agent identification, plus a centralized registry of locally available MCP servers to be included with the OS.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Isolate agentic tools.</span></strong><span> Microsoft is building an OS-agnostic isolation mechanism that should make it easy for developers to build agents that run tools safely.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Running models locally</span></strong><span>: Windows is betting big on local models. WindowsML is a new hardware abstraction layer for building and running local AI models across GPU, NPU, and CPU. The OS aims to ship Small Language Models (SLMs) without requiring an NPU in the future. We’ve also seen an impressive demo of a local model running on a Surface laptop using NVIDIA chips.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Building agents on Windows:</span></strong><span> one goal of the OS is to allow building of agents with opinionated frameworks and libraries that devs can just assume are available.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>More dev-friendly</span></strong><span>: Windows was plagued by questionable product decisions that resulted in a cluttered Start menu and search, to the chagrin of many developers who lost interest in the OS. Microsoft wants them back and is addressing criticisms – </span><em><span>finally!</span></em></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Linux on Windows (WSL): </span></strong><span>Windows ships with an embedded Linux called Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). It’s proving quite popular with devs. Windows embracing Linux might just be the strategy to get devs to switch from both native Linux and macOS, as counter-intuitive as this strategy sounds.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Windows & hardware:</span></strong><span> since its early days, Windows has gone out of its way to support a wide variety of hardware. The OS was x86-based from the beginning, but Windows on ARM is starting to finally look like a good alternative. A look into why ARM support took so long, and the upcoming NVIDIA collaboration.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We’ve talked with people on the Windows team to learn about the thinking behind Microsoft’s strategy for the operating system: Pavan Davuluri (EVP, Windows and Devices), Scott Hanselman (VP, Member of Technical Staff, Microsoft CoreAI and GitHub), and Logan Iyer, (CVP, Windows Platform and Developer). </span><em><span>Many thanks for your time!</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: Agent identity & discovery</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At the operating system level, agents increasingly look like regular users. Their sessions can last hours, use multiple programs, and use OS resources like the UI and clipboard. Windows allows developers to build agentic programs that are distinguishable from users.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Agent identification</span></strong><span> is enabled through </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dcca0083-34f5-46d6-82e9-2815fd9b1f8e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Entra ID</span></a><span>, Microsoft’s tool for centralized identity management in Windows. When an agent has a local identity, it acts as if it is another user on the system as visible in the Task Manager. Below, tasks are grouped by user, and there are two users in the task manager: kirupach (a human) and V9-G4 (an agent). All observability of human users is now available for agent users as well.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure underline;"><span>Source</span></a><span>: Microsoft</span></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Agent href="https://substack.com/redirect/5da3e203-f14b-40a5-8e08-6a254207b87f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>ODR</span></a><span>) is the centralized place where agents register and discover available MCP tools. ODR manages and runs MCP servers locally, and also comes with connectors for core operating system components like the File Explorer or System Settings.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let’s say you want to build a specialized Photo Organizer Agent; the organizer agent organizes photos in the user’s Photos folders by theme and starts by running an image classifier to understand photos’ themes, then puts them in the relevant folder, such as ‘</span><em><span>parties</span></em><span>’, ‘</span><em><span>outdoors</span></em><span>’, ‘</span><em><span>baby photos</span></em><span>’, etc.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As such, the Photo Organizer Agent needs the ability to read and change the user’s local files, which starts with Windows ODR finding an MCP connector for the file access capability. After discovering File Explorer, the agent uses File Explorer MCP to access and modify files in the user’s Photo directory.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: This is a useful choke point because it enables Windows to detect potentially dangerous behavior. However, this proxying behaviour is as yet unconfirmed by Microsoft, so it remains to be seen how they use it.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>3. Isolate agentic tools</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Tools are external programs that an agent uses to perform actions on the operating system, such as native OS tools, third-party app calls, or even programs written by an agent. Granting agents rights to execute tools potentially means code execution, so it’s essential the agent tools run in isolation to ensure the user’s files and session aren’t reachable by agentic tools.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Microsoft Execution Containers</span></strong><span> (</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aef28adb-0819-406e-9e24-0aec5ff80526?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>MXC</span></a><span>) is a new, in-development agent containment technology by Windows. Developers can use MXC to spawn agentic tools in isolated environments called sandboxes, and agent access within the sandbox environment is configured through MXC </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/02a904fa-9ced-4046-a278-14d9b478a820?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>containment policies</span></a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Containment policies are JSON-based config files that describe network, filesystem, UI, and execution restrictions. The image below illustrates how MXC works:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 different containment tech & OSes</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let’s say you’re building an agentic application like OpenClaw. This application will necessarily have to use tools to do its job and can use file operations, web operations, shell commands, and more. These are potentially dangerous operations, as OpenClaw executes them through MXC’s spawnSandboxFromConfig() method, which spawns a new contained process in which said tools can run safely. The process containment technology used depends on the containment policy config. MXC doesn’t do the containment itself and uses multiple existing containment technologies for that; for example, on a Mac, it would use </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f8888044-39f9-4d8e-b3a6-00624c94b39b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>seatbelt</span></a><span>, a process containment layer built into the Mac OS.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Speed versus safety tradeoff: </span></strong><span>some containment mechanisms are faster to start and cheaper to run than others. For example, starting a new process is faster than starting a new Windows session or a new virtual machine. At the same time, running a new process in the existing user’s Windows session potentially exposes the user’s filesystem to the new process.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>MXC allows developers to adapt the containment level to the sensitivity of the operation being run. Multiple containment levels are available in Windows:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Process containment</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Session containment</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Running WSL containers</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Lightweight Hyper-V containers</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Full virtual machines</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Choosing the right level of containment is a trade-off between the blast radius and speed of execution. agents</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These cases illustrate how Microsoft is automating many internal developer chores, and how MXC provides finegrained control over agent isolation. MXC is under development, but already runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS. Developers therefore get a unified way of containing external tools across operating systems.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>4. Running models locally</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e132cbc6-d8f0-41e5-b847-5a7712c250f8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Windows ML</span></a></strong><span> is a hardware-agnostic layer for running AI models locally on Windows. Its goal is to do for AI what DirectX did for computer graphics: abstract away hardware complexity, regardless of the underlying model’s architecture.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Windows ML is Microsoft’s second attempt at building a hardware-agnostic layer for running ML models. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0f6c2145-b586-4925-8bed-f94132c565b6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>DirectML</span></a><span>, the first attempt, is a library for running machine learning tasks on GPUs built on top of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5a22ab27-4ff2-4a8f-b3b8-b11afb09ada1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>DirectX 12</span></a><span>, Microsoft’s graphics library used for running games on Windows, released in 2019.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So, an obvious question is how is Windows ML different? They say that Windows ML offers two improvements over DirectML:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>#1: Higher level abstraction & better hardware coverage</span></strong><span>. DirectML is a low-level library where developers have to manually build the inference pipelines from simple mathematical operations, worry about memory layout, etc. Being based on DirectX, DirectML only worked with GPUs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In contrast, Windows ML is based on the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8c653bbd-199d-4690-8d4a-47440d36afb5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Open Neural Network Exchange format</span></a><span> (ONNX), an open format for representing and running neural networks. Neural networks built with all popular machine learning frameworks can be converted into the ONNX format called ONNX graph and run on </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/eabf5226-275d-45c9-900f-59fc4261fedf?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>ONNX runtime</span></a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>ONNX runtime is an open source, cross-platform system for training and running neural nets defined in the ONNX format. Windows ML provides developers a framework that runs on a broader range of silicon, including GPUs, NPUs, and CPUs from all major vendors.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>#2: No driver-update bottleneck:</span></strong><span> Windows ML wraps the ONNX runtime and abstracts away the hardware-specific runtime optimizations by providing hardware-agnostic APIs. Each hardware vendor implements this API for its own hardware through the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9e899d05-155d-49f7-9979-7b998c18acc3?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Execution providers</span></a><span> (EPs) concept. With DirectML, new runtime optimizations had to be done via driver updates which took six months to get meaningful adoption.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Windows ML loads EPs when they are needed, depending on the user’s hardware. For example, if a user has an NVIDIA GeForce RTX GPU, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7a375fca-fa6f-4dc1-8224-54fe25446e08?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>the NVIDIA Tensor RTX execution provider</span></a><span> is downloaded and used to maximize GPU performance. Hardware vendors build and submit PEs to Microsoft for certification and testing before they can be used with Windows ML. Most execution providers </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dfcb20c7-ce5f-4ac0-a8bf-a74a8a55026f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>available today</span></a><span> are also available on GitHub.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: underline;"><span>Small language models</span></a></strong><span> (SLMs) are embedded within the operating system. On top of incurring app running costs, it can also add lag to the app, whereas with embedded models developers can assume the models are already there, and use them as any other local library. </span><br><br><span>For example, </span></span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b40816a9-cb00-495b-b43e-37c33f166dfb?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>the Aion-1.0-Instruct model</span></a><span> is built into Edge, Microsoft’s web browser. application can now have LLM-powered features like sentiment analysis without having to continuously pay for tokens. The demo is JavaScript-only, but versions for native apps and other languages are also expected to be available when it’s released.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Teams being able to run their own models is becoming increasingly important, especially in the corporate sector, driven by escalating costs, mode availability questions such </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/443fde75-4527-46f5-935f-839f54a8c3be?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>as those recently raised with Fable</span></a><span>, and compliance issues.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Running models locally also unlocks a hybrid approach, which is well aligned with a trend among tech companies we </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/362cd763-34b9-488c-a6ee-4dca0b487c44?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>recently covered</span></a><span>, where tech companies have successfully shifted their LLM workloads to cheaper models for simpler requests, and only use frontier models for advanced reasoning. By running models locally, some agentic jobs could be executed with local LLMs, and more complex jobs delegated to a cloud-hosted frontier model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Running local models on a next-gen Surface laptop with NVIDIA GPUs is impressive. </span></strong><span>At Microsoft, Scott Hanselman showed us a pre-release Surface laptop with NVIDIA GPUs running Qwen as a local model, hooked up to GitHub Copilot. This local model churned out tokens at a rate of ~40 tokens per second! Once such laptops become widely available, coding-related use cases could become a lot more viable, running locally.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>5. Building agents on Windows</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Besides Windows being agent-friendly, Microsoft is also investing in the agent building toolchain to simplify agentic app development by providing a rich agent building framework.</span></p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f45d3b79-6ca8-4a5e-9afd-28256feca533?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Microsoft Agent Framework</span></a></strong><span> (MAF) is a C#, Python, and Go library designed to make it easy to build agents on Windows. More than just a wrapper around LLM APIs, the framework supports agentic primitives like tools, multi-turn conversations, persisted memory, and even a workflow engine. It’s the main option for .NET developers and integrates well with agentic primitives in Windows mentioned earlier. The following snippet illustrates how easy it is to use MAF primitives:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure functions that your agent can then use as tools, which is explicitly mandated via instructions passed in the system prompt. You don’t have to stitch together old message exchanges to keep the agent’s context up to date; the built-in session capability handles it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>MAF natively supports all the above-mentioned agentic primitives that the OS ships with. Developers can use it to build native agentic apps for Windows which in turn comes with useful agentic primitives built into the OS.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Windows being an opinionated runtime environment for agents has a few advantages for developers who build agents:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Simpler to build Windows-native agents.</span></strong><span> Developers can assume certain agentic capabilities in the OS. For example, local MCP capabilities can be discovered and registered via ODR, and there’s a simple way to contain tool execution.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Support to run local LLM models.</span></strong><span> Windows ML will make it easy for developers to include custom local AI models within their apps. Previously, developers had to consider hardware variants and bundle different SDKs with their app. Windows ML should abstract all of that away.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Company-level agent administration.</span></strong><span> Larger companies can have control over agents in their enterprise. Whitelists dictate which agents can run, limit what access they have, and have observability of agents in the network.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>6. More dev-friendly</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As alluded to by the existence of terms like ‘Microslop’, Windows isn’t such a popular operating system among software developers these days. This is a change from when the OS couldn’t be avoided during its </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/62fd7e3d-9fe9-43e8-886f-28b2d68320d2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>XP</span></a><span> era, when Windows enjoyed a 90+% market share. But that changed as apps transitioned to web and mobile, driven by two forces:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Switching operating systems easier than ever</span></strong><span>. Most modern apps are web based and run on any OS. Before, when considering a switch to a new OS, you had to check if your favorite desktop apps worked. This is no longer an issue as modern desktop apps are on the web, or use cross-platform frameworks like </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fe742241-c5f2-41cf-a6d8-322bb71f128f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Electron</span></a><span>.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Windows got less developer-friendly. </span></strong><span>Windows became less configurable over time, with stricter requirements on what users could do – exactly the things developers dislike. Also, command line support lagged behind Unix-based operating systems, and Microsoft kept ignoring developers’ configurability complaints.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Basically, developers were frustrated with Windows as they felt it wasn’t prioritizing their use cases. For example, OS configurability, flexibility, and system details that developers value were largely ignored:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Mandatory Microsoft accounts: </span></strong><span>these became compulsory with Windows 11. Windows is the only OS to mandate a vendor-specific account to use an OS. With macOS, an Apple account is only needed to use Apple services; the OS can be used without one.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Clutter and ads: </span></strong><span>The start menu and Windows search grew cluttered with irrelevant content like app suggestions, web search results, and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7edbd9a2-9cd5-4e6f-93b4-a8a7131aa312?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>even ads</span></a><span>, with no way to change things.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Lack of customization:</span></strong><span> With Windows 11, customization of the taskbar’s size, position, auto-hide, and similar tweaks, were no longer possible</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Since then, the Windows team seems to have gotten the memo that devs dislike all the above changes, and Windows chief Pavan Davuluri </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4862ca6c-3638-40f0-b15f-375f271ac06d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>committed</span></a><span> to making Windows better for developers. Now, there’s now less clutter in the start and search menus, and Windows simplified its most used menus. Non-critical features are now optional:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Start menu size can be changed and no longer has to occupy the whole screen, which is critical on smaller laptops.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Various tips and app recommendations can now be removed from the Start menu</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Here’s an example of how broken Windows Search was, until recently. </span></strong><span>Below, a user searches for a text file (“New Text Document”) that contains the word “motorola”. Before, on the left-hand side, Windows Search returned too many irrelevant web results and suggestions. But after a recent change, it now returns only the relevant document.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure The overall operation can last an hour or more, but the whole process is hands-off for the user.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Microsoft Account still required:</span></strong><span> Frustratingly for some users, a fresh Windows installation </span><em><span>still</span></em><span> requires a Microsoft account. While </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e10dcf87-19ea-45e1-9004-16f96c826e25?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>multiple</span></a><span> </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/de06a652-9755-4b2a-9b6f-a0ad31b4f499?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>bypasses</span></a><span> exist, we fail to see how such a strict requirement can make Windows attractive to devs when no other OS mandates a vendor-specific account just to install it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Being forced to log into an account like this is annoying, but the privacy controversy over the ‘Recall’ feature dealt a major blow to Microsoft’s already-damaged reputation with devs: </span></strong><span>In May 2024, Microsoft </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/45207783-e6b0-4436-b299-ed3baf882f54?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>announced</span></a><span> Recall, a Windows feature that allows users to search their previous activity. Recall took screenshots of the desktop every few seconds, indexed them, and made them searchable. It was marketed as a photographic memory for a computer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There were two major problems with this:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>No ability to turn it off:</span></strong><span> Microsoft </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/22b8e125-6f4f-4d60-8fd1-e5b96e1685a5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>wanted</span></a><span> to make the feature non-removable, using resources on all machines, whether or not a dev wanted to use the privacy-invading feature.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Comical security approach</span></strong><span>: Recall shipped with a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3c480b6f-56f7-420c-b561-f58b47451d18?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>serious security flaw</span></a><span>. Screenshots did not remove sensitive information like banking data or other personal data, and all the information was kept in a local SQLite database in plaintext! That meant any local app or rogue user could read the data without the user’s consent or knowledge.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s unclear why Microsoft thought it would be acceptable to ship a poorly implemented, privacy-invading feature without an opt out. Microsoft later </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ac93ff8c-7c10-46c9-b898-5ab036f4a8e2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>cancelled</span></a><span> the June 2024 general launch of Recall, and the final version was released to the public in April 2025, as an opt-in, non-mandatory, feature. But much damage was already done. Why would devs trust an OS vendor that shipped core OS features so carelessly, and only changed course after large – and predictable! – public uproar?</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>7. Linux on Windows (WSL)</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Historically, developer tools were </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5d7f975b-df1e-4947-ad42-cb83740efac7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Microsoft’s strong suit</span></a><span>; after all, its very first product was a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2ac896b4-08c2-400f-807a-423bf9465567?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>BASIC interpreter</span></a><span>. Throughout the 1990s and 2000s, Visual Studio was the gold-standard IDE for building desktop applications: fast and snappy at a time when competing IDEs like Eclipse or NetBeans were painfully slow. Until around 2010, the Visual Studio debugger was the industry standard for debugging tooling.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But Microsoft’s development tools became less popular as the tech industry focus moved from desktop apps to web apps, and later to mobile apps. The issue was that Microsoft’s tools were Windows-only, while web and mobile apps were built using open source technologies. So, developers increasingly chose Mac or Linux. In response, Microsoft is making Windows more Unix friendly to try and win developers back.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) has addressed the issue by shipping Windows with an embedded Linux since 2016. With WSL, Linux is accessible in Windows by typing wsl in the command prompt. Previously, running Windows and Linux on the same machine required </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6a064d46-018d-4bfc-bb73-95df2bc5a334?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>dual-booting</span></a><span>, and during that process the user had to pick which operating system to use. Switching back to the other OS required a reboot, and sharing data between the two operating systems was cumbersome. Linux could read or write Windows disks, but not vice versa.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>WSL doesn’t just run Linux inside Windows. It has also allowed running native Windows apps from WSL for a few years now. For example, let’s say you have the following a web server access log file:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>WSL is proving popular with developers.</span></strong><span> Scott Hanselman told us:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Linux on Desktop is already happening, it’s just running inside Windows.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Jon Seager, VP Engineering at Canonical working on Ubuntu </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/de2c4526-d7e3-4ff0-9132-55e30e5f75b3?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>told us a similar story in April</span></a><span>, of Ubuntu adoption through WSL growing significantly faster than general Ubuntu desktop adoption, and how it expects more Windows-based machines to run Ubuntu than “native” machines running the Linux distribution!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are a few reasons why WSL became popular with devs:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Use the same stack that production runs on. </span></strong><span>Most servers run on Linux. Building software for Linux on Windows without WSL is possible, but in most cases it adds a layer of unneeded complexity. Developers want to build in an environment that resembles production as much as possible, and WSL makes this possible.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Work on a gaming PC: </span></strong><span>many devs still have Windows boxes, but they just don’t use them for work. Instead, they’re for gaming because Windows has a big videogame library. WSL allows them to use the Windows box the same way they would use their work computer. Since the gaming PCs often have good GPUs, they can be used as CUDA dev boxes through WSL. Building with CUDA is possible without WSL, but the production environment is Linux.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Developing for Linux services</span></strong><span>: as one example, building Kubernetes applications on Windows previously meant running virtual machines inside Windows. VMs are slow and take up more memory than running the service in the OS itself. With WSL, Kubernetes can run on Windows without this VM overhead.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Microsoft’s goal is to make Windows a place where getting developer tasks done is easy. A task can require a Linux or a Windows tool, or a combination of both, but it should still be easy. As further evidence that Microsoft is committed to this, Windows recently added a native </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/99396ea1-a421-43d5-89a2-11d40a7157a2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>coreutils implementation</span></a><span>. With this, it’s possible to run standard UNIX utilities like cat, head, tail, sort, and uniq inside of a Windows terminal, even without WSL.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Containers are another Unix primitive coming to Windows.</span></strong><span> </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/90762aab-5009-4eeb-8a2c-4dfe887e5f30?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Containerized apps</span></a><span> have been an industry standard for building and shipping software since the late 2010s, and the launch of Docker. Windows has supported Docker Desktop through WSL since ~2019. But the recently announced </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/416b6705-e9b1-4ea5-807d-9d970f6c6e0a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>WSL Container</span></a><span> takes Docker support in Windows further:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It provides a Windows native drop-in replacement for the docker CLI</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>It comes with an API that Windows apps can use to manipulate containers directly from the application code</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The common theme of these launches is that Microsoft is trying to make Windows interesting to developers once more by supporting both Unix and native Windows-style development. Making standard Unix tools available certainly is a big step forward. However, it’s still necessary to address other accumulated grievances which devs have.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>8. Windows & Hardware</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>From the 1990s, Windows had a symbiotic relationship with Intel called </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2453132e-208a-40ce-b411-673847793dcc?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Wintel</span></a><span>, which was an interplay of:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>New CPUs enabling newer versions of Windows: most famously 386 CPUs enabling Windows 3.0</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Windows requirements driving hardware consolidation. Most notable examples included </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/62821160-92f8-42cd-8ad2-64f75cffd3c7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>PnP</span></a><span> for automated hardware installation with Windows 95, UEFI Secure boot with Windows 8, TPM 2.0 security standard with Windows 11</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It wasn’t always an easy relationship. For example, when CPUs became 64bit, Intel built a new architecture with its Itanium CPUs, and AMD chose a backward-compatible x64 architecture. Windows ran without changes on AMD’s design and Itanium required all software to be rebuilt for it. Windows adoption helped AMD’s approach to win out, and Intel discontinued the Itanium line in 2021.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Windows-on-ARM saga</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>ARM processors are more energy efficient than x86 CPUs, while ARM based laptops have longer battery life, and are quiet since they do not need fans for cooling. Windows has been tied to x86 CPUs since the 1990s, so running the OS on ARM is challenging as supporting ARM processors requires more than just recompiling the OS from source code. It also requires changing the kernel architecture to run efficiently on them.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Needing so many changes is why it took multiple attempts and more than a decade to get Windows to run well on ARM with good app availability. Here’s an overview of the Windows-on-ARM story:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Windows RT (~2012)</span></strong><span>: a tablet-focused fork of Windows never meant to fully replace it on laptops. There was no way to run standard Windows apps on Windows RT, so the platform didn’t get traction and was later abandoned.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Windows 10 on ARM (~2017)</span></strong><span>: Microsoft went for full x86 compatibility through a realtime translation engine. The translation performance was poor and excessively drained batteries when running x86 apps, and couldn’t execute x64 apps at all. The industry largely abandoned 32-bit software, so popular apps like Adobe Photoshop and web browsers like Chrome couldn’t even run on this OS. This approach was abandoned for Windows 11.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Windows 11 on ARM (~2024):</span></strong><span> a new emulation engine called </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/16faa744-1b44-4b5d-901c-7f61f33e4938?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Prism</span></a><span> improved the emulation performance and finally supported 64 bit applications. This makes apps running in emulated mode more responsive, making the ARM transition possible.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Interestingly, Linux has similar ARM adoption problems, despite the fact that most of its software is already open source. While open source apps are available for ARM64 Linux, the main problems are with proprietary, closed-source apps. For example, Chrome became available for ARM on Linux in early August 2026.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Part of the problem with the Windows-10-on-ARM attempt was that the chips these machines were running were in essence mobile phone CPUs; underpowered and unsuited for the heavy workloads expected of a Windows workstation. With Windows 11, Microsoft partnered with Qualcomm and later, NVIDIA, to design stronger chips, which are natively equipped with NPUs and are part of the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4c7af742-8cd5-48cb-9d16-9f8ae371cb1c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Copilot+ PC specification</span></a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Copilot+ PC specification was introduced in 2024, with the goal to define the baseline for what a “good” PC for running local AI workloads looks like. Microsoft attempted to achieve two things with Copilot+ PC spec:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>push hardware manufacturers towards enabling new AI experiences in Windows</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>use its Windows install base strategically to get AI engineers to run their LLMs locally.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Two years on, it’s fair to ask why Copilot+ PCs didn’t really take off. There have been a few roadblocks:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Lack of games: </span></strong><span>Some popular games depend on kernel level anti-cheat functionality that still doesn’t work on ARM</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Price premium: </span></strong><span>Copilot+ PCs are more expensive than the average Windows laptop</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>NPUs didn’t take off yet:</span></strong><span> Most Copilot+ PC functionality has since become available on all Windows 11 PCs with GPUs, so there is no edge to having an NPU.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Battery life improvements seem to be the biggest win for the first generation of Copilot+ PCs, with users reporting over 20 hours of video playback and 15+ hours of regular computer usage.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>NVIDIA collaboration</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Microsoft and NVIDIA announced the RTX Spark chip in early June of this year. RTX Spark combines an ARM based 20 core CPU (</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/61354a97-281e-4f92-9b86-a8e468c3b690?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Grace CPU</span></a><span>) and NVIDIA’s Blackwell GPU on the same chip. Machines equipped with this hardware have capacity for running and training AI models locally, and NVIDIA claims 1 Petaflop of 4-bit floating point precision.</span></p><div 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em><span>Announcement slide from NVIDIA, showcasing RTX Spark performance. Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9a78d584-f8a2-4097-98f5-bc9b0f2db4ec?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>NVIDIA</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This time, Microsoft was more than just an OS provider; it </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d1bf4be2-1c93-43e2-aa37-1a98783485b1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>claims</span></a><span> close collaboration with NVIDIA to ensure Windows works well on the new silicon. With the strong compute capacity, increased battery life, and improved x64 app performance, RTX Spark based machines look like a compelling Windows machine on paper.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Still, success is not a given, as we’ve seen with Copilot+ PCs before, which </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/83390f9e-6233-4f9a-91ef-46b69dd673e2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>was a bust</span></a><span> in demand terms.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Key questions will again include gaming support, and whether the hardware delivers on its promise; for example, no battery performance numbers have yet been published. Microsoft is betting that developers will like it because models are easy to run locally, while the hardware capability should make it fast.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today, industry sentiment is different than in 2024 when Copilot+ PCs launched. Nobody seriously talked about local inference back then, whereas today, major players </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/59d39f16-27a9-4d81-baef-7209de7cd314?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>are already doing it</span></a><span>, primarily driven by cost concerns. In the local inference demo that Scott Hanselman showed us, we saw that at 40 tokens per second the performance is usable for daily dev work.</span></p><h1 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(2em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Takeaways</span></h1><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Our sense is that Windows has gone from being the most popular “developer operating system” in the early 2010s, to possibly being the least popular choice to build software on – at least within startups! –, by 2026. Much of this decline seems to come from the Windows team fumbling the ARM transition – which Apple got very right! – deprioritizing power users, and shipping features that upset devs, like the mandatory Microsoft login.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Microsoft seems to be frantically trying to win back devs, but is it too late? </span></strong><span>Our sense is that Microsoft is attempting to put its developer division “A-team” on Windows, to add features that could woo devs back to the platform. It’s great to see longtime advocates for devs like Scott Hanselman working for Windows, and smaller experience improvements </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4862ca6c-3638-40f0-b15f-375f271ac06d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>shipping</span></a><span> on it, but the question arises as to why Microsoft was content to make the power-user, developer experience worse every year, until recently?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Linux seems to be Microsoft’s strategy to get devs to use Windows more. </span></strong><span>Talking with devs, WSL is the most beloved part of Windows. By making Linux seamless to run on a Windows machine, devs can do most of their work on Linux, while running on hardware that Windows machines support.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One of the strengths of Windows has always been its expansive hardware partnerships and driver support. Even today, the Windows team is probably the single biggest OS development team in the tech industry, and a good part of this team is dedicated to ensuring broad hardware support. And so devs can buy a beefy Windows machine to play games on, and then just spin up their favorite Linux distribution when it comes to getting work done.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Local AI inference is another big bet. </span></strong><span>Our sense is that it’s a matter of “when” and not “if” good enough local AI models will run on laptops. Token costs are an ongoing concern at tech companies, and having decent, fully local coding models run on laptops could be a big win for everyday coding use cases. Microsoft is a company without a frontier model, so has additional incentive to make local inference a reality. We’ll keep our eyes on Microsoft’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6d0e8b1f-91de-4e25-9a71-4f4db1cbaaeb?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>7 October event</span></a><span> with NVIDIA, where it’s likely to announce a machine with cutting-edge local AI capabilities.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The “agent-friendly” Windows is an opinionated OS approach, and we appreciate Microsoft having an honest go at it. </span></strong><span>AI agents are here to stay: not just for software engineering, but for general knowledge work. Our sense, from </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5fbd9f4f-221c-4370-b5d5-cc3105dc680e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>talking with Ubuntu</span></a><span>, is that the leading Linux distribution is more of a “wait-and-see” approach when it comes to adding potential agentic primitives to the OS.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Windows team, on the other hand, decided to make agents a new primitive: starting by giving them their own identity within the operating system, adding layers of isolation, and iterating on this approach. We expect Microsoft to change its direction quite a bit in the coming months and years because all this is new, and it’s unlikely that Microsoft – or any other OS maker! – will get the primitives right at the first try.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s encouraging that the Windows team is leaning into open source when it comes to agents: MXC and Microsoft Agent Framework are open source and support other operating systems. And Windows ML leverages ONNX, which is also an open, cross-platform standard.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Are OSes becoming less important, overall, for us developers? </span></strong><span>This is a fair question to ask in closing. More AI coding agents are adding cloud support, and at companies like Ramp and Uber, devs run most of their AI harnesses inside cloud environments. Many apps we use for coordinating and planning development – ticketing, documenting, monitoring, or even oncall – are either web apps, or cross-platform apps that run on all major operating systems: macOS, Windows and Linux alike.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this world, how much does an OS really matter? Our suspicion is that it’s probably far less than before – and it could well be hardware capability, configuration, and cost that become more important in choosing workstations.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, competition in the OS space is great for developers. For the first time in a long time, Microsoft seems to be the underdog in the dev OS space for devs, so it will surely compete harder than ever, which should mean users will win. Let’s see if Microsoft’s renewed efforts will be enough to woo more devs back to Windows. Good luck to the Windows team in attempting to pull this off! </span><em><span>Thanks again to everyone at Microsoft who contributed to this article!</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>What is your take on using Windows for professional development? Leave a comment below with your observations.</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;hanging-punctuation: allow-end;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>This post is only for paying subscribers of </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIxNjkyNzIyOSwicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3OTAwOTc3ODgsImV4cCI6MjEwNTY3Mzc4OCwiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.ubDHS4OTUHDzA2TFzGmi3V3CUgIdpK9TO4Vq_G28gwg?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The detector has a challenging job. If it detects too early, it cuts the user off in the middle of a thought. If it decides too late, users experience awkward delays. Interruptions face the same challenge. When users start talking over the voice system, a separate mechanism has to stop the audio and clear the buffers. If the interruption detection is too sensitive, spurious interruptions can be triggered from background noise. If detection is too conservative, interruptions take too long and feel sluggish, while short interjections like “yes” and “no” can be entirely missed. Justin points to this machinery as the reason earlier voice systems felt unnatural.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Full-duplex Architecture</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Full-duplex models are designed so they can both listen and talk simultaneously. The model continuously produces audio tokens. When it should stay silent, it simply produces silent tokens. Similarly, it continuously processes the input audio tokens. When the user is silent, those are just silent tokens. This design removes the turn detector entirely.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To better understand, let’s use an open full-duplex model, Moshi [x], as a reference. Moshi converts audio into discrete tokens, similar to how text is converted to tokens for LLMs. The model processes these tokens as inputs and emits new tokens on a fixed clock, roughly one frame every 80 milliseconds. Silence is simply another token that decodes to silence. So the model just needs to learn the behavior during training and implicitly understand when to listen and when to talk from the training data.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" engineering challenges. First, since the model is always running and predicting the next token, serving is costly. Second, the model needs to respond within milliseconds, so it cannot be too large in capacity.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenAI launched GPT-Live-1 in July 2026, a family of full-duplex voice models. It is designed around the challenges described above. The voice model stays small and fast so it can respond within milliseconds. It also relies on delegation to perform expensive reasoning while the conversation keeps going.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How the GPT-Live System Works</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This section explains how OpenAI managed to build a voice assistant around a full-duplex architecture. We cover the ideas and techniques that make it practical at scale in production.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Separating Talking from Thinking</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Normally, a frontier LLM might reason, search the web, and then respond, which can take several seconds. In voice systems, that translates to a few seconds of silence, which is not ideal.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To fix this, OpenAI separates talking from thinking. A voice model handles the conversation with the user. Another capable model performs the necessary reasoning and tool calling for more complex queries. The serving system is also built around this idea. It delegates the request to the capable model when needed, while continuing the conversation with the user.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>The Two Serving Paths</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Serving two models is tricky. Audio frames should be sent every few milliseconds, but a delegation can take seconds. So we cannot have a shared process for both. GPT-Live splits the traffic. The live path carries audio only. It moves audio between the client and the voice model as fast as possible. The async path handles anything other than the audio, which can take longer. This way, a slow tool call may delay the async path but not the live path.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>How to make the live path fast?</span></h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The main requirement of the live path is that audio must move between the user and the model on a fixed clock. The model processes frames as input and produces them as output in real time. So the user hears a delay when it occurs. As Zahan explains, whenever a bottleneck makes the system fall behind, it starts producing audible artifacts.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To meet this requirement, lots of optimizations are needed. For example, the connection must open quickly, the model must keep up with the incoming stream, and frames must be delivered on time. Here are a few engineering techniques OpenAI adopted to keep the live path fast:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Starting a session in one round trip</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Having cheap continuous inference</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Handing off live conversations between model instances</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>1. Starting a session in one round trip</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When the user taps the voice button, the client must establish a connection before any audio can flow. This requires a few network trips, depending on the underlying protocol. GPT-Live uses WebRTC, which is used in most video calling apps. But a standard WebRTC session takes six steps to establish before a single audio frame can be sent. On a mobile network where one round trip takes 60 milliseconds, setup alone can cost over a third of a second.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size:
