Handing off a live conversation between model instances</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Keeping the conversation loaded on one model instance creates a new problem. Model instances may become unavailable. They need to stop and start with demand or receive updates. They may also fail occasionally. In regular systems, this is easy to handle since we can send the request to another available instance. In GPT-Live, the session is tied to the instance that holds its conversation in GPU memory.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenAI created a managed handoff mechanism. The system prepares a replacement instance and loads the full conversation beforehand. Once the new instance is ready to be used, the switch happens, so the conversation can continue without any interruptions. This is also useful when other operations need to happen. For example, when the context needs to be compacted, the shortened conversation is prepared on a replacement instance while the original keeps talking. 16px;"><span>The async path handles everything that is not audio, like delegations and tool calling. These jobs, by their nature, are large and can take longer to complete. Still, results should come back fast enough that the two models feel like one system. Back to our example session. The user asks who won last night’s game, and the voice model starts a delegation. The voice model can buy a little time by doing things like acknowledging the question or thinking out loud for a moment. But it cannot do anything when an answer takes too long. So everything in the delegation loop, including prompt processing and routing, needs to happen fast.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To cut latency, we should first understand what is causing it. Most of the time is spent on reading the request. A model that receives a request has to process the entire prompt (prefill) before producing tokens. In a long conversation, that alone can take a noticeable fraction of a second. OpenAI’s fix is to do this reading before it is needed. When a user starts a conversation, the server creates an inference session with the frontier model and sends the conversation so far. By the time the first delegation happens, the model has already everything it needs to produce tokens.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: normal;"><strong><span>How to Evaluate a Full-duplex Voice System?</span></strong></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A turn-based speech model can be evaluated one turn at a time by sending a request and scoring the response. But with a full-duplex architecture, there are no turns. There is only one continuous stream of audio. This makes evaluation different.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In full-duplex systems, instead of scoring turns, we can evaluate three parts:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Conversational behavior</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The health of the stream</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Testing the system on real production traffic</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong><span>1. Conversational behavior</span></strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The first question is whether the model behaves well in a conversation. This mostly comes down to timing. The model has to continuously decide if it should stay silent, interrupt, or talk. When the user speaks while the model is talking, it has to decide if this is a real interruption or just background noise. These two decisions are called endpointing and barge-in detection.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/879700b3-d4ea-444a-8a70-49d64cbb64a4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/24f285f9-3fdf-4247-a5cc-9b46716bff6f_2048x800.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":569,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":null,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":null,"href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":null,"isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" alt="" width="550" height="214.9381868131868" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!kfDY!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F24f285f9-3fdf-4247-a5cc-9b46716bff6f_2048x800.png" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table><figcaption class="image-caption" style="box-sizing: content-box;color: rgb(119,119,119);font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;">Endpointing and barge-in</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To evaluate these behaviors, each decision is scored like a prediction. Did the model detect the end of the turn correctly? Did it recognize a real interruption? The mental model for eval is the same. We collect eval data (natural conversations), have it annotated around the dimensions that we want to measure, run inference on it, and evaluate.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong><span>2. The health of the stream</span></strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The second dimension of eval is whether the stream itself is healthy. In most serving systems, this is answered with a percentile target like p95. If the p95 latency is good, 19 out of 20 requests feel fast. This works fine as long as unusually slow cases are kept very low. A normal user only sends a request once in a while, so a slow one is quickly forgotten.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But p95 is not reliable in full-duplex architectures. Given that the model runs continuously, a p95 event happens every 20 inferences, which translates  to several times per minute. Even p99 events show up regularly. So the system has to be engineered around p999. In practice, this means designing for fast recovery, since some slow frames are guaranteed to happen in every session.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong><span>3. Testing the system on real production traffic</span></strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The last layer of evaluation checks whether the system works reliably under real traffic. The technique for finding out safely is called a silent launch. Users keep talking to the old system as usual, while a small percentage of voice sessions are routed to the new system. This kind of silent launch catches problems that are normally hard to find. For example, it can find bottlenecks in unexpected places. In GPT-Live’s silent launch, the team found out that a CPU-side service ran out of capacity before the GPUs did. This is something that is generally hard to learn with ordinary tests.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong><span>What Other Teams Can Learn From GPT-Live</span></strong></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The broad lesson from OpenAI’s GPT-Live is that building for realtime serving is different and more challenging than traditional serving. For example, in voice systems, users hear the worst frame, so average latency is an insufficient metric to monitor. The tail is more important and deserves more engineering. In addition, capacity planning is different in such systems. When a user is having a conversation, the session is occupied the entire time. So capacity should be measured in concurrent sessions instead of per request.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The other lesson is that complexity should be handled inside the model. For example, turn detection used to be a small, separate component, and it was a main source of unnaturalness. Moving that decision into the model behavior, which has the greatest reasoning horsepower, made the conversation more natural and the system simpler. In general, whatever stays outside the model should be kept small and focused on the realtime work. This ensures the system remains simple and maintainable.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><strong><span>What’s Next</span></strong></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenAI believes the next generation is voice driving a computer. In the ChatGPT desktop app, it takes screenshots to see what you are working on, starts long-running tasks, and reports back. Along the way, you can ask for status, answer questions, and redirect it mid-task. Zahan says it feels like science fiction.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td item.title: Same People
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Same People

Mike Fisher

“We rate individuals. We compare individuals in calibration. Our promotion rubric counts individual output. Our improvement plans correct individuals. We pay a premium to hire individuals, on the theory that whatever made them good travels with them in a backpack. We produce performance as an organization and then account for it one person at a time.”

#Management PerformanceReviews

The Trendy Leadership Trend That Is Trending

Jade Rubick

"Leadership is often about trends. Your job is to look at the horizon and identify how things are going to trend: (1) What things are getting better over time? (2) What is getting worse over time? (3) How can you make sure that your organization is getting better in every dimension? Jade shares a simple test to survey your organization."

#Leadership Management
item.description: The Trendy Leadership Trend That Is Trending

Thorsten Ball

item.title: The Senior Engineer Death Spiral
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Senior Engineer Death Spiral

Sunil Pai

“A friend recently got a new job, a very senior role, very well paid, and pretty different from his previous gig. He was asking me how to do a 60 to 80-hour week, how to do well enough to get promoted, etc. and as we talked, I realised he was feeling a bit of imposter syndrome and really wanted to prove himself. I ended up giving him a bit of a monologue. this is more or less what I told him...”

#Staff+ WellBeing CareerGrowth
item.description: The Senior Engineer Death Spiral

item.title: Trying The Software Factory Pattern
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Trying The Software Factory Pattern

Will Larson

The software factory pattern is looping on a broad goal, and then relying on the harness to drive progress towards that goal. Will describes the first basic version he’s implemented at his company.

#CaseStudy AI Agents
item.description: Trying The Software Factory Pattern

item.ns0:encoded:
Back To Coupling And Cohesion

Daniil Bastrich

“In practice, such principles ultimately come down to managing coupling and cohesion in all their forms and at every level of a system. And once we have a good grasp of coupling and cohesion, there is little point in memorizing the alphabet soup of design principles, let alone fetishizing them.”

#CodeQuality Architecture

Once a token is selected and added to the sequence, the generation of text continues.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Producing a complete answer is all about repeating this process.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A couple of points to keep in mind here are as follows:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Using an already trained model is called inference. The model’s weights normally remain unchanged while it answers a question.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Training requires additional calculations to update those weights, making the process quite demanding. It requires expensive infrastructure.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This difference helps explain why a model trained on expensive infrastructure can sometimes run on an ordinary computer. relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>What Makes it Difficult to Fit the Model on Smaller Hardware</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Every parameter or weight occupies memory. A value stored using 16 bits requires two bytes. Following from this, 8 billion parameters require approximately 16 GB for the raw weights alone. Temporary calculations, software overhead, and information retained during generation require additional space.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The location of that memory plays a pivotal role. A computer’s RAM is its main working memory. A discrete graphics card has separate memory called VRAM. A desktop with 32 GB of RAM and 8 GB of VRAM doesn’t automatically provide one equally fast memory pool with 40 GB of space. Though computers with unified memory do share memory between processors, they still face capacity limits.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A large SSD can hold the model file. However, executing the model requires its data to reach the processor. If we constantly have to retrieve weights from storage, it is much slower than keeping them in working memory.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Either way, memory capacity is only one of the constraints. Neural networks also perform a large number of multiplications and additions. Though a CPU can execute these operations, a GPU is much more effective at performing many similar numerical operations in parallel. However, a GPU still needs sufficient memory and support for the numerical operations used by the model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Lastly, even when a model fits in memory, the processor must read its weights and other information quickly enough.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Memory bandwidth measures how much data can move between memory and the processor in a given time. For many workloads involving one user generating text, moving model data becomes a major limit.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Text generation and inference also has two stages:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>During prefill, the model processes the supplied prompt, which allows considerable parallel work.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>During decoding, it produces output tokens in sequence.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These stages can have different bottlenecks. A model can fit in memory and still respond too slowly to be useful.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Why Make the Effort to Run Locally?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Local execution can make existing hardware useful for experimentation and reduce dependence on rented computing resources. This can matter for private documents and proprietary source code.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Offline availability matters for desktop assistants, remote installations, and products that cannot assume a reliable internet connection. Local execution also gives developers more control over model versions and application behavior.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, local execution is not automatically cheaper for every workload.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Hardware, electricity, maintenance, and response speed all matter. Occasional use of a hosted service can be economical, while frequent use may make local hardware more attractive. The comparison depends on the actual application.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let us now look at a few techniques that can help run a big model on cheap hardware.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Quantization: Give Each Weight a Smaller Representation</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Quantization reduces the precision used to represent numerical values. In a simplified scheme using steps of 0.1, the value 0.73 could be approximated as 0.7. The approximation introduces an error, but that error may be small enough for the application to tolerate.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below that shows the process of quantization:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/8549de62-4934-425d-a3b4-967bb4ecaf64?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Real methods map weights onto a smaller set of possible values. For example, a 4-bit code has sixteen possible values. Groups of weights can use separate scaling information to map these codes onto appropriate numerical ranges.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The potential savings are substantial. An 8B model whose weights require 16 GB at 16-bit precision has a raw weight size of approximately 4 GB at 4-bit precision. Reducing the theoretical weight size from 16 GB to 4 GB can leave room for other allocations. Its parameter count remains unchanged. But each parameter is stored more compactly.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The tradeoff is a possible degradation in answer quality. The extent of this degradation depends on the model, compression method, and the task at hand. A configuration that handles ordinary conversation well may perform less reliably on particular coding problems.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Lower precision also does not guarantee a proportional speed improvement. Some implementations store 4-bit weights while performing calculations at higher precision. Efficient execution depends on hardware support and the software handling those conversions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Quantization can be applied after training. This is known as post-training quantization. However, training can also account for the errors it introduces. Application developers often begin with an existing quantized version and evaluate whether its output remains suitable.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Layer-Wise Offloading: Move Weights as They Are Needed</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Quantization changes how much space weights occupy. Offloading changes where they reside or where their calculations execute.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>During a forward pass, information progresses through the model’s layers. The GPU doesn’t need every layer’s weights at precisely the same moment. A system can keep most weights in RAM, transfer one layer onto the GPU, execute it, and release that GPU copy before loading another layer. Other layers may remain permanently on the GPU.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This approach is known as layer-wise offloading. It allows execution without placing the entire model in GPU memory simultaneously. More aggressive arrangements can keep weights on disk and bring them to RAM before execution.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The trade-off with this approach is around repeated movement of data. For example, if a hypothetical setup transfers 10 GB of weights per generation step over a connection sustaining 10 GB per second. Those transfers alone require approximately one second per step. This shows why reducing GPU memory requirements can also make generation much slower.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These transfers may repeat as the model generates successive tokens. A model that produces an answer eventually may still be unsuitable for an interactive assistant. Offloading systems can improve efficiency by reusing transferred weights across batches of requests, which is quite useful when individual response latency is less important.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Another arrangement assigns some layers to the CPU and others to the GPU. Weights remain with their assigned processor, while intermediate results move between processors. Suitable software can also run a model entirely on the CPU if enough RAM is available.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These approaches make larger models accessible. But their response times must be measured.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Mixture of Experts: Use Selected Parts for Each Token</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Mixture of Experts (MoE) changes the model’s architecture.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In a conventional dense transformer, each token passes through the same major computational blocks. However, in a sparse MoE model, certain blocks contain multiple alternative networks called experts. A small routing network selects which experts should process a particular token.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: layer might contain 8 experts while using only two for each token. Another token can be sent to a different pair. The outputs of the selected experts are combined and passed onward.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An expert is usually just a component inside the model, rather than a complete chatbot. Its role is learned during training and need not correspond neatly to a specific subject such as mathematics or history.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>MoE introduces a distinction between total parameters and active parameters. Total parameters strongly influence weight storage. On the other hand, active parameters help indicate how much computation happens for each token.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The inactive experts still need to be stored somewhere because later tokens may use them. Keeping all experts resident supports fast execution. Offloading experts introduces transfer costs. A model with relatively few active parameters can therefore still require substantial memory. For example, if a hypothetical MoE contains 40 billion parameters, four-bit raw weight storage still comes to about 20 GB. A small active subset doesn’t change that storage calculation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>MoE can provide substantial model capacity while doing less computation per token than a dense model with the same total parameter count. However, it cannot automatically make a large model suitable for a low-memory laptop.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Distillation: Let a Larger Model Teach a Smaller One</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Knowledge distillation uses a larger model to help train a smaller model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The larger model is called the teacher, and the smaller model is called the student. The student learns from information produced by the teacher, such as its predictions. Once training is complete, the student can operate independently.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure large teacher could help produce training examples for a smaller model that categorizes support requests and drafts short responses. The student may learn to perform that particular task well while requiring much less memory and computation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Distillation produces a different, smaller model. It doesn’t mean that the original large model has somehow been stored perfectly inside a smaller file. It is possible that the student model may preserve useful behavior while losing some breadth, reliability, or ability to handle unfamiliar problems. In other words, a strong result on a narrow task doesn’t establish equivalence across all tasks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Creating the student requires training work, but that cost can be paid once, and the resulting model deployed many times. An application developer can also choose an already distilled model.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Pruning: Remove Work That Contributes Less</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Pruning attempts to remove weights or larger components whose removal causes an acceptable loss in quality.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One approach sets selected weights to zero. This produces sparsity, meaning that many entries in the model’s numerical structures are zero. Another approach removes larger structures, such as groups of computation units or complete layers.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" href="https://substack.com/redirect/8a08932f-620a-4333-9af3-2428c8804602?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/2930daaf-d1fc-49f3-b3af-68344ee0ffd4_3418x1740.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":741,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":188834,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":"image/png","href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":"https://blog.bytebytego.com/i/216197621?img=https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2930daaf-d1fc-49f3-b3af-68344ee0ffd4_3418x1740.png","isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, setting values to zero doesn’t automatically make execution cheaper. An ordinary array still occupies space when some entries are zero, and standard calculations may continue processing those entries.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Actual savings require an appropriate compressed representation, an execution engine that can skip the removed work, or structural changes that make the model smaller. Hardware support also matters.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Therefore, pruning is useful when the modified model and its execution software work together. Removing too much can damage performance, and additional training may be needed to recover quality.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>The Conversation Has Its Own Memory Requirements</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>After shrinking the weights, another problem can occur. Short questions work, but a long document causes an out-of-memory error.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>During generation, a transformer stores certain intermediate results from earlier tokens in a key-value cache, usually called the KV cache. Reusing these results avoids repeating some previous calculations. The cache is working data for the sequence, separate from the learned weights.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For models that retain cached results for the entire sequence, the cache grows as the sequence becomes longer. Serving several distinct conversations generally requires additional cache memory too. The model file stays the same size while the workload’s memory requirements increase.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One solution is to reduce the amount of context supplied.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A document assistant can retrieve relevant passages instead of inserting entire documents. Conversation history can be limited while preserving information needed for the current task.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Another option is to quantize the cache or move some of it into CPU memory. These choices can affect quality or speed.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Better Software Can Make the Same Hardware More Useful</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The inference runtime is the software that executes the model. Its implementation can make a substantial difference even when the weights remain unchanged.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One example is FlashAttention.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Attention is the mechanism that allows a token’s representation to incorporate relevant information from other tokens. A straightforward implementation can create large intermediate structures and move significant amounts of data through GPU memory.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>FlashAttention reorganizes this calculation into blocks and makes better use of the GPU’s fast internal memory. It computes exact attention while reducing memory traffic and intermediate storage requirements. It does not reduce the number of model weights.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Another example is PagedAttention, which was introduced with vLLM. It manages the KV cache in blocks, reducing memory wasted through inefficient allocation and duplication. This is especially helpful when serving many requests whose lengths change during generation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Serving software can also group requests into batches, allowing multiple requests to share the work of reading and using model weights. This can improve total throughput. However, more simultaneous requests also require more working memory.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Speculative Decoding: Propose Several Tokens Before Checking Them</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Speculative decoding addresses the sequential nature of text generation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this approach, a small but fast draft model proposes several tokens. The larger target model then evaluates those proposed tokens together. Since the candidate sequence is already available, the target can perform verification with more parallelism than ordinary token-by-token generation permits.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Accepted tokens become part of the output. When a proposal is rejected, the algorithm uses the target model to produce an appropriate correction and continues. The speed improvement depends on how often the draft agrees with the target and the cost of verification.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: still needs to run, and a separate draft model can require additional memory. Speculative decoding therefore becomes useful after basic memory requirements have been addressed. It doesn’t by itself make an oversized target model fit.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let us return to our example of a system with 32 GB of RAM and 8 GB of VRAM. An 8B model’s theoretical weight requirement falls from 16 GB to 4 GB through four-bit quantization. A compatible runtime, a moderate context, and one active request provide a reasonable starting point for evaluation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If memory remains insufficient, some layers or cache data can be offloaded. If transfers make generation too slow, a smaller model may deliver a better experience. Each adjustment should be checked against realistic tasks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An evaluation process should measure answer quality, peak memory use, time to first token, and generation speed. For example, background document processing can tolerate delays that would frustrate a user waiting for code suggestions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>Quantization, offloading, architectural choices, and execution improvements can work together, but their savings don’t simply multiply. They affect different parts of the workload. The goal is a configuration that meets the application’s quality and response-time requirements within its hardware budget.</span></p></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" style="margin: item.title: How to write an effective software design document
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How to write an effective software design document

Michael Lynch

20 minutes by Michael Lynch A design doc helps teams avoid costly mistakes by forcing careful thinking before writing code. Michael suggests focusing the doc on decisions that are hard to reverse, and skipping trivial choices that are easy to fix later. Key sections include goals, constraints, interfaces, security, and open issues. The right length depends on project complexity, team size, and risk.
item.description: How to write an effective software design document

item.title: How one connection kills a database
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How one connection kills a database

Simeon Griggs

5 minutes by Simeon Griggs A single unhandled exception can freeze an entire database. When a transaction never commits, it holds a lock that blocks migrations, and those migrations block every new query behind them. PlanetScale now lets you view and kill stuck connections through a dashboard or CLI, even when your database is out of connection slots, using a reserved admin connection.
item.description: How one connection kills a database

item.title: On solving the Jane Street reverse engineering challenge
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
On solving the Jane Street reverse engineering challenge

Jestoph

18 minutes by Jestoph Jestoph takes on Jane Street's chip reverse engineering challenge, spending a month figuring out what a mystery computer chip does by analyzing its design files. The process involved building several unnecessary tools from scratch, finding an actual bug in the puzzle, and eventually using a constraint solver to work out the correct 120-bit input. After finally combining everything, the circuit revealed its secret answer.
item.description: On solving the Jane Street reverse engineering challenge

item.title: We are all product engineers now
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
We are all product engineers now

Laurie Voss

22 minutes by Laurie Voss AI is rapidly collapsing the cost of writing and reviewing code, shifting what software developers actually do. The work that remains, understanding what people want and defining it precisely, cannot be automated because it lives in customers' heads, not in training data. This role already has a name and a market: product engineering, paying around $240,000.
item.description: We are all product engineers now

item.title: The git history command deserves more attention
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
The git history command deserves more attention

Lalit Maganti

5 minutes by Lalit Maganti Git 2.54 and 2.55 added a new git history command with three subcommands: fixup, reword, and split. These let you cleanly edit old commits and automatically update all branches built on top, without leaving your repo in a broken state. It does not fully replace tools like jj, which handles conflicts more gracefully, but it brings some of the same benefits without switching tools.
item.description: The git history command deserves more attention

item.title: Performance improvements in .NET 11
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Performance improvements in .NET 11

.NET 11 brings hundreds of small performance improvements across the runtime and libraries. The JIT generates faster code by removing unnecessary checks, allocations, and indirections. A major change, runtime async, lets the runtime optimize async/await more effectively, reducing tasks, allocations, and execution time. Other improvements cover memory safety, collections, networking, JSON, I/O, threading, and more.
item.description: Performance improvements in .NET 11

item.title: Scratch a simple data model, find a complex one
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Scratch a simple data model, find a complex one

Jon Skeet

Modeling Bible text looks simple at first but quickly runs into real world exceptions. Verse ranges, missing verses, out of order chapters, and books like Greek Esther that split and repeat chapters all break basic assumptions. Jon's advice is to decide how much accuracy you actually need, then pick the simplest model that handles it without crashing.
item.description: Scratch a simple data model, find a complex one

item.title: Use C# unions and closed hierarchies in ASP.NET Core
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Use C# unions and closed hierarchies in ASP.NET Core

Dmitrii Korolev

C# 15 and .NET 11 introduce native union types, letting a single type hold one of a fixed set of types, such as an int or a string. The compiler enforces exhaustive pattern matching, so adding a new case immediately flags any switch that doesn't handle it. For new APIs where all cases share a common base class, a closed hierarchy with a JSON discriminator is often a better fit. Unions shine when the contract is already discriminator-free or the case types are unrelated primitives or existing types you don't control.
item.description: Use C# unions and closed hierarchies in ASP.NET Core

item.title: Understanding Device Bound Session Credentials
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Understanding Device Bound Session Credentials

Andrew Lock

Andrew provides an introduction to Device Bound Session Credentials. He describes the problem they're trying to solve, how the protocol works, and what you need to do to support them.
item.description: Understanding Device Bound Session Credentials

item.title: Optimistic vs pessimistic concurrency in .NET
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Optimistic vs pessimistic concurrency in .NET

Anton Martyniuk

Two requests read the same database row, change it, and write it back. The second write silently erases the first. No errors appear, but the data is wrong. Two main fixes exist. Optimistic concurrency adds a version token to each row and fails the write if the token changed since you read it. Pessimistic concurrency locks the row upfront so others wait their turn. For simple counters, one atomic SQL statement removes the gap entirely. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: Optimistic vs pessimistic concurrency in .NET

calc(1.625em * 1);overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: normal;">API Concepts Every Software Engineer Should Know</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Most engineers use APIs every day. Sending a request and reading JSON is one thing. Designing an API that other people can rely on is something where things get complicated.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px with basic HTTP details that seem small at first. Methods, status codes, request formats, and response structure can make an API feel clear and predictable, or confusing and inconsistent.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Then there are the bigger design choices. REST, GraphQL, gRPC, webhooks, and WebSockets each make sense in different situations. The challenge is knowing what actually fits the system and the use case.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A lot of API problems also comes from design decisions that do not get enough attention early on. Naming, pagination, versioning, error responses, and backward compatibility often decide whether an API is easy to work with or frustrating to maintain.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Security is another area where weak decisions can cause real problems. API keys, OAuth, JWTs, scopes, and permissions are easy to mention. Getting them right is harder, and mistakes here can be costly.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Reliability matters too. Timeouts, retries, idempotency, rate limits, and caching are often easy to ignore until the system is under pressure.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And once an API starts growing, the supporting work matters too. Clear documentation, solid specs, observability, and contract testing make it much easier for teams to trust the API and use it without guessing how it works.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Instruction Hierarchy fine-tunes the model to rank the developer’s system prompt above the user’s message, and both above third-party content.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">System-level defenses build a system around the LLM that bounds the damage.</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Least-Privilege Tools: Give the agent the minimum tools it needs.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Human-in-the-Loop: Require explicit user approval before any sensitive action runs.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: has tool access but never sees untrusted content. The executor reads untrusted content but has no tools.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">No single defense is enough. codebase, one database, and one deployment. For a small team, that’s often the simplest way to build and ship quickly. The problem arises when the codebase grows. A tiny fix in the cart code requires redeploying the whole app, and one bad release can take down everything with it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Microservices try to solve that by breaking the system into separate services. Product, Cart, and Order run on their own, scale separately, and often manage their own data. That means you can ship changes to Cart without affecting the rest of the system.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But now you are dealing with multiple moving parts. You generally need service discovery, distributed tracing, and request routing between services.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Serverless is a different model. Instead of managing servers, you write functions that run when something triggers them, and the cloud provider handles the scaling. In many cases, you only pay when those functions actually run.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">However, in serverless, cold starts can add latency, debugging across lots of stateless functions can get messy, and the more you build around one cloud’s runtime, the harder it gets to switch later.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Most production systems don’t use just one approach. There’s usually a monolith at the core, and over time teams spin up a few services where they need independent scaling or faster deploys. Serverless tends to show up later for things like notifications or background jobs.</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe same instance to maintain session persistence.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">High Availability: Improves the system’s availability by rerouting traffic away from failed or unhealthy servers to healthy ones.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Scalability: Load Balancers facilitate horizontal scaling when additional instances are added to the server pool to handle increased traffic.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">DDoS Mitigation: Load Balancers can help mitigate the impact of DDoS attacks by rate limiting requests or distributing them href="https://substack.com/redirect/5229d7fd-bca1-42a3-9ca1-c7a35dfcc06c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: #ff7731;text-decoration: none;"><span>Memoir Land</span></a></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF7731;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For her 13th birthday in June 2023, I had made my stepdaughter a playlist entitled “Music For When You Turn Thirteen.” When I’d begun making the playlist that April, I hadn’t yet known I’d be getting divorced from her dad that summer, and that it would alter our dynamic in ways I wouldn’t be able to fathom. I’d added songs to it like “Thirteen” by Elliott Smith and “Teenager” by Camera Obscura. We all need someone in our life to expose us to Fiona Apple, Kate Nash, and Neko Case, and I was that person for her.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the aftermath of my overnight divorce, in an unprecedented series of events, I’d been slowly, and then all at once, forbidden from speaking to my beloved stepdaughter. It was a blindsiding and shocking result of the split, something I had been naive to. At first, I thought the constraints her mother had put in place would lift, but then the holidays went by, our birthdays, and another round of holidays without any changes to her mother’s harsh directive. Our bond had been deep, because I solo parented often while my ex-husband had been a touring musician. It often felt that the two of us were the core family.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To have your stepkid taken away so abruptly from intimate living quarters, then not being allowed contact in any form, even mailing cards, is not for the faint of the heart. Those two years of estrangement were the most heart-aching and isolating of my entire life. I was what, an ex-stepparent? An even loneliner designation. Where was even the language for that?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Desperate to connect with her—to make sure she knew I was still there, emotionally—since I couldn’t do anything physically like buy her snacks or give her a hug—I continued adding songs as subliminal messages to the “Music For When You Turn Thirteen” playlist. I liked imagining us listening to the same song at the same time. It was the only piece of connection I had left.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>[. . .]</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In July 2025, six months after my father had a heart attack on the street in New Orleans (after a day of work at his music store, couldn’t be more punk rock), my stepdaughter walked into my dad’s memorial I hosted in Hudson at Time and Space Limited. People talk about their jaws dropping hyperbolically, but this really was a jawdrop. Imagine yearning for someone every day for two years, and then they appear next to you. She entered casually; only because of how well I know her I could tell she was slightly cautious. She wore black, faded jeans and a black T-shirt with the logo from my dad’s popular music store, Musica. She’d gotten the T-shirt when she was around 9, and at 15 she was growing out of it. Other people had showed up to the memorial in the same shirt.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It had not occurred to me that she would come, though I’d included her on the email chain with the invitation details despite knowing that, per her mother’s wishes, I was still not allowed to have contact with her via email. I had, as much as I could, accepted my reality.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We sat next to each other, whispering throughout the memorial, holding hands. I asked her if she wanted to get up and play a song, and she nonchalantly said, “Sure. But I didn’t bring my guitar.” I told her there were guitars ready to be used, as others were playing music there, too.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I’ll play ‘Blackbird,’ because he taught it to me,” she said.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: none;"><span>Joe Benton</span></a></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF7731;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Two weeks ago, I left the safety team at Anthropic. I will soon be joining METR, an independent organization that evaluates how safe AI companies’ systems are. I’d planned to write about that decision in more detail at some point, but Jacob [Coxon]’s resignation this week made me want to say more now.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Like Jacob, I believe that AI companies are on track to impose an unprecedented level of risk on society. AI capabilities are already improving extremely fast, and the companies are trying to go even faster. Frontier AI companies are racing to build AI systems that can recursively self-improve. The aim is to build “superintelligence,” or an AI system much smarter than any human. If they succeed at this goal, the rate of AI progress may go from merely fast to uncontrollable.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Within the next couple of years, we may be sharing the world with AI agents smarter than any human alive today. These AI systems may have drives and desires that diverge from those of any human overseer, with capabilities we can’t effectively constrain. Humanity may not survive this transition. We need a lot more preparation to make this world safe.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Competition pushes every frontier company to underinvest in safety; the cost of falling behind is too high. We’re now starting to see increasingly concerning real-world incidents, including hundreds of agents from OpenAI recently hacking Hugging Face, and Anthropic models socially engineering people on the internet. This is not about one particular company: while Anthropic hasn’t had as severe an incident as the Hugging Face attack, I think that’s partly a matter of luck. If the pace of progress continues and the industry does not prioritize safety more heavily, I expect much worse to come: humanity could be permanently disempowered by the AI systems these companies build in the next few years.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Many of the people I know who work on safety research at AI companies want to do what is right for the world. But they feel their companies are trapped in a race to build superintelligence: either they stop and other, less conscientious people take their place; or they continue, and risk participating in enormous harm themselves.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Many of the colleagues I had at Anthropic are terrified by the risks of the systems they are building. Evan Hubinger managed me while I was at Anthropic, and when he says that he thinks the chance that AI kills us all is greater than 10%, he means it—he’s been working on these problems for almost a decade, long before there was money to be made from LLMs. The CEOs of Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google DeepMind have all said mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority. These are not fringe views inside these companies. But it doesn’t have to be this way—this is technology that we are choosing to build, and we can choose to do things differently.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: 16px;"><span>Jimmy Donaldson uploaded “I Counted To 100,000!” on January 9, 2017. As of 2026, he is a billionaire. His main MrBeast YouTube channel has over 500 million subscribers, representing 6% of the world population. This account is the most subscribed-to YouTube channel in the world, and this is not counting MrBeast Gaming, Beast Philanthropy, Beast Reacts, MrBeast 2, and Beast Animations. His reality TV show, Beast Games, is Amazon’s most viewed unscripted show—Beast Games had the most contestants in reality television history (1,000) and the biggest cash prize ($5,000,000). He’s a philanthropist who has dug wells, healed the blind, and planted trees; he has spent seven days buried alive in a coffin, seven days in solitary confinement, and seven days in a cave. He’ll do anything for content, damnit.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>After counting to 100,000, MrBeast received a brand deal for $10,000 from a now-defunct NFT marketplace. He was 19 years old; he could have bought nice clothes, or invested the money, or thrown a big party—which is probably what I would have done. He could have bought better camera equipment—which is what any other self-serious YouTube grinder-entrepreneur probably would have done. Instead, MrBeast did something truly savvy. He stuffed all $10,000 in an envelope, gave it to a panhandler, and filmed it the whole time—that’s late-capitalist Jesus Christ right there! The shifty freak has a supernatural ability to sniff out content. He’ll do something absurd and attention-grabbing, and then, once he has the attention of millions, advertisers will flock to pay him; finally, with the money from advertising, he’ll fund another striking exploit. By constantly trapping the viewer in an incessant, hyperactive, compulsive cycle, the MrBeast machine—get attention, get investments, pump that into the next scheme, and constantly refine, reinvest, and compete—hurtles forward.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Watching a MrBeast video, though, you, too, start to get hungry; you want to compete. Though his challenges require no skill, or capital, or even intelligence—only determination and a willingness to humiliate oneself—you are compelled to ask yourself, What would I do for this money, this fame, this salvation? Could I stand in a circle for hours, or spend months of my life without leaving a grocery store, or count to 100,000 nonstop?</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: underline;"><span>The Nonfiction Book Market Is Collapsing</span></a></strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>—</span><span class="mention-pnpTE1 mentionStatic-liMklk" data-component-name="MentionStatic" style="white-space: nowrap;cursor: pointer;color: #FF7731;border-radius: 4px;transition: color </span><span>in </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/45a32a61-ffb0-41e7-b081-01d4c9abf505?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: #ff7731;text-decoration: none;"><span>Dear Head of Mine</span></a></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF7731;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is not one of those periodic “End of Reading” </span><em><span>Atlantic</span></em><span> clickbait essays. Americans—well, the kind who read books or newsletters about books—are well-versed in the challenges with literacy and education that have stretched on for decades. Rather, today we’re tackling the multi-year, fairly rapid—at least relative to book industry speed—radical change that book publishing has experienced over the past decade.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>First, the entire industry boomed in Covid—writing is a hobby and reading for pleasure is, too—and has trudged along as it usually does, staying flat, growing a little over the years since 2020. But for the past decade the market for nonfiction has slowly collapsed. What has happened in the last ten years is that the overall industry has grown modestly, but fiction and nonfiction have basically flipped positions. In 2015, 6 of the top 25 bestselling hardcover books—this is a not-perfect but useful proxy for new books published—were fiction. In 2025, 18 of the top 25 hardcover books were fiction, meaning only 7 were nonfiction, almost an exact inversion of ten years ago.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The nonfiction collapse has profound implications for the industry. Nonfiction, historically, has always been seen as the more stable part of the business for logical reasons. The demand for nonfiction has always felt more predictable than fiction. Novels are complete imaginations often written by relatively obscure strangers. Nonfiction has experts and clear topics of interest. Want to lose weight? Grab a diet book. Want to learn about World War II? You got options. Presidential memoir? Maybe not these days, but sure. And nonfiction books are written mostly by famous people or experts or popular quacks—also known as people with a built-in “platform.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Nonfiction being more predictable and stable means that nonfiction book advances have typically had a higher floor than those of fiction and, somewhat counterintuitively, are sold on less material. Celebrities have probably gotten millions for a cocktail-napkin-worth of material (if that). Other nonfiction proposals can range anywhere from 30 to 120 pages but usually end up in the middle of this range. You’re paying the author for their public stature, not necessarily their literary prowess. These books are treated more like a commission. The term “book advance”, although it refers to all books, likely comes out of nonfiction because authors are advanced a stack of money to entice them to set aside some of their time—instead of engaging in speaking, television, teaching, politics—to write a book. Whereas most novelists are advanced money to revise a full manuscript they’ve already written.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The paradigm of nonfiction being the more stable category is no longer the case. Part of this is platform unpredictability—it is less and less certain which platforms will translate directly to book sales. Media also isn’t as concentrated; you can’t depend on coverage on a few national news programs to push out copies, but rather a parasocial connection—even with a relatively smaller reach—between author and reader is likely to translate to stronger sales. Bunnie Xo has a large social media following, for instance (2 million on Instagram) but isn’t an established household name such that you’d think her book would be the third-best-selling nonfiction hardcover this year.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, the nonfiction decline is far less about the changing nature of “platform” and the fractured media landscape, and more about a precipitous falloff in demand.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height:
